questions.subtopic: IT Steering Committee. Definition and Purpose
questions.question: An IS auditor reviews the charter of a new IT steering committee. Which stated responsibility BEST reflects the committee's PRIMARY purpose?

options.A: Monitoring the day-to-day delivery of individual IT projects
options.B: Reviewing weekly help desk tickets and incident counts
options.C: Prioritizing IT investments against enterprise strategy
options.D: Obtaining external expert validation of the IT roadmap

questions.key_concept: An IT steering committee is a cross-functional senior body that prioritizes IT investment and keeps IT aligned with enterprise strategy.
questions.pre_read: Think about who sits on the committee and why. Ask which duty needs senior business and IT leaders together.
questions.correct_explanation: The steering committee brings senior business and IT leaders together to set priorities, allocate investment and keep IT aligned with enterprise strategy. Monitoring projects is close, because committees do track major programs, but day-to-day delivery belongs to project management; the committee's distinctive value is deciding which investments best serve the business.

wrong_explanations.A: Day-to-day project tracking is a project management duty. The committee oversees the portfolio and steps in on major issues.
wrong_explanations.B: Ticket and incident counts are operational metrics reviewed by IT service management, not a senior alignment body.
wrong_explanations.D: External validation may inform the roadmap, but the committee's role is internal prioritization and alignment.

tips: Eliminate: B is operational service reporting, and D describes an outside advisory body, not the committee's purpose.
Final two: C beats A because the committee aligns and prioritizes investment; day-to-day delivery is a management task.
Exam cue: steering committee answers point to alignment, prioritization and investment, never to operational detail.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 EDM01 (Ensured Governance Framework Setting and Maintenance); COBIT 2019 APO05 (Managed Portfolio); COBIT 2019 APO02 (Managed Strategy)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'IT Steering Committee foundational definition - cross-functional senior alignment body, distinct from d2_003 (application tier) which addressed proper composition design'. Public source: COBIT 2019 + ISACA EGIT. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.subtopic: HR Management. IT-specific Training Program Design
questions.question: An IS auditor reviews a manufacturer's IT training program. Which design feature MOST strongly supports IT staff competence over time?

options.A: One annual company-wide session with identical content for each role
options.B: Training scheduled whenever incidents expose a team's skill gaps
options.C: Funded vendor product certifications for each technical role
options.D: Role-based skill-gap assessments with targeted plans and reassessment

questions.key_concept: Sustained IT competence comes from role-based competency frameworks, individual gap assessment, targeted training and periodic reassessment.
questions.pre_read: Notice the words over time. Ask which design finds gaps before they cause problems and checks they stay closed.
questions.correct_explanation: Competence is sustained when each role's required skills are defined, individual gaps are assessed, training targets those gaps and competence is reassessed periodically. Vendor certifications are valuable and current, but they cover products rather than the full set of skills each role needs, and they do not show whether a specific person's gaps were found and closed.

wrong_explanations.A: Identical annual content ignores role differences and skill levels, so most staff get little that matches their real gaps.
wrong_explanations.B: Waiting for incidents means gaps cause harm before they are addressed. Training stays reactive.
wrong_explanations.C: Product certifications are useful, but they do not assess role-wide competence or track individual gaps over time.

tips: Eliminate: A ignores role differences, and B waits for incidents to reveal gaps.
Final two: D beats C because it measures and closes each person's role gaps; certifications cover products only.
Exam cue: for competence questions, prefer the answer that assesses gaps, targets training and re-checks results.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 APO07 (Managed Human Resources); NIST SP 800-181 Rev 1 (NICE Workforce Framework)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'IT-specific HR training program design - role-based + individualized + refreshable, distinct from d2_018 (fraud-risk HR controls) and d1_044 (audit team training)'. Public source: COBIT 2019 APO07. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.subtopic: Outsourcing Strategies. Onshore vs Near-shore vs Offshore
questions.question: A bank's IT management is choosing between near-shore and offshore development partners. Which factor MOST strongly favors near-shore?

options.A: Closer time-zone overlap for real-time work with business users
options.B: Lower hourly labor rates than typical offshore outsourcing providers
options.C: Lower travel costs for periodic on-site vendor oversight and audit visits
options.D: Freedom from cross-border data-transfer safeguards and reviews

questions.key_concept: Near-shore trades some cost advantage for easier collaboration: closer time zones, smaller cultural gaps and easier travel than offshore.
questions.pre_read: Recall what offshore usually wins on. Ask what near-shore offers that offshore cannot.
questions.correct_explanation: Near-shore partners sit in nearby countries, so working hours overlap and business users can collaborate in real time, which supports alignment with business needs. Offshore usually wins on cost and scale. Lower travel cost is also a near-shore benefit, but it helps only occasional visits; daily overlap with business users is what keeps delivery aligned.

wrong_explanations.B: Offshore locations typically offer the lowest labor rates. Near-shore usually costs more than offshore and less than onshore.
wrong_explanations.C: Cheaper travel is a real near-shore benefit, but it eases occasional oversight visits; time-zone overlap enables the daily collaboration that keeps delivery aligned.
wrong_explanations.D: Data still crosses a national border. Transfer safeguards, contracts and regulatory review still apply.

tips: Eliminate: B is an offshore advantage, and D is wrong because near-shore is still cross-border.
Final two: A beats C because daily real-time collaboration drives alignment, while cheaper travel only eases occasional visits.
Exam cue: offshore = lowest cost and scale; near-shore = collaboration at moderate cost; onshore = closest control at highest cost.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Vendor Management Audit/Assurance Program; COBIT 2019 APO10 (Managed Vendors)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Outsourcing geography - cost-vs-collaboration trade-off near-shore as middle ground, distinct from d2_017 (multi-factor outsourcing decision) and d2_041 (in-house retention drivers)'. Public source: ISACA IT Outsourcing Strategy guidance. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.subtopic: Cloud Risk Management. Beyond Shared Responsibility
questions.question: An IS auditor evaluates a financial firm's cloud risk program, which already documents the shared-responsibility split. Which control MOST strengthens ongoing cloud risk management?

options.A: Annual procurement review confirming contract terms still hold
options.B: A penetration test performed before the original cloud migration
options.C: Continuous configuration monitoring against an approved baseline
options.D: Annual review of the provider's SOC 2 Type II report

questions.key_concept: Beyond the responsibility split, cloud risk needs continuous evidence that the customer's own configurations stay within an approved baseline.
questions.pre_read: Notice the word ongoing. Ask which side of the shared-responsibility split the firm itself must keep proving.
questions.correct_explanation: Most cloud incidents stem from customer-side misconfiguration, which is the firm's own responsibility and can change daily. Continuous monitoring against an approved baseline gives ongoing evidence that those controls remain in place. A SOC 2 Type II review is still worthwhile, but it covers the provider's controls over a past period, not the firm's own configurations.

wrong_explanations.A: Confirming contract terms still hold says nothing about whether cloud controls are working. It is an administrative check, not risk evidence.
wrong_explanations.B: A pre-migration test is point-in-time evidence that ages quickly as the environment changes.
wrong_explanations.D: A SOC 2 report covers the provider's side over a past period. It gives no assurance over the firm's own configurations.

tips: Eliminate: A checks paperwork, and B is a single point-in-time test that ages quickly.
Final two: C beats D because the firm must evidence its own side continuously; SOC 2 covers the provider's side.
Exam cue: in cloud questions, match evidence to the responsible party; the customer's configurations need the customer's own ongoing evidence.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Cloud Computing Management Audit/Assurance Program; CSA Cloud Controls Matrix; FFIEC Joint Statement on Security in a Cloud Computing Environment (2020); COBIT 2019 APO12 (Managed Risk)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Cloud Risk Management beyond shared-responsibility - continuous evidence pipeline, distinct from d2_014 (shared-responsibility split) and d2_049 (data ownership in cloud)'. Public source: ISACA Cloud Risk Management + CSA CCM + FFIEC. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.subtopic: Risk Management Program Stand-up. Governance Design
questions.question: An insurer's management is launching its first formal IT risk management program. Which element MOST supports the program's long-term sustainability?

options.A: A detailed risk register compiled once during program launch
options.B: Advanced quantitative modeling software driving every risk decision
options.C: An external consultancy owning the register and running reviews
options.D: A named manager responsible for keeping the register current

questions.key_concept: Risk programs last when an accountable internal owner keeps them current; expertise can be bought, but accountability cannot be outsourced.
questions.pre_read: Think about what keeps a program running after the launch team moves on. Ask where accountability sits.
questions.correct_explanation: Sustainability comes from accountability inside the organization: a named manager keeps the register current, drives reviews and answers for results after the launch team moves on. An external consultancy is tempting for a first program because of its expertise, but accountability for managing risk cannot be outsourced; when the engagement ends, the organization is left without ownership or capability.

wrong_explanations.A: A register built once goes stale as risks change. Without a refresh cycle it soon misleads decision-makers.
wrong_explanations.B: Tools support analysis, but software cannot set appetite, assign accountability or keep the program running.
wrong_explanations.C: Consultants can advise, but risk ownership must stay inside the organization. Outsourcing it leaves no lasting accountability.

tips: Eliminate: A goes stale after launch, and B relies on a tool rather than governance.
Final two: D beats C because accountability for risk stays in-house; consultants can advise but cannot own the program.
Exam cue: for sustainability questions, pick governance and accountability over tools, documents or outsourced effort.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Risk IT Framework; COSO ERM (2017); COBIT 2019 APO12 (Managed Risk)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Risk Mgmt Program standup governance design - cadence + owner + appetite + integration + feedback, distinct from d2_011 (5-component program structure) and d2_007 (risk lifecycle gap analysis)'. Public source: ISACA Risk IT + COSO ERM 2017. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.subtopic: Senior Management and Boards. IT Governance Roles
questions.question: An IS auditor assesses IT governance roles at a listed company against COBIT 2019. Which division of responsibility BEST reflects the board's role?

options.A: Board approves the design and schedule of each major IT project
options.B: Board evaluates, directs and monitors; management plans, builds and runs
options.C: Board and executive management share identical IT governance accountabilities
options.D: Board runs IT operations while management reviews them yearly

questions.key_concept: COBIT 2019 separates governance (Evaluate, Direct and Monitor) by the board from management (Plan, Build, Run and Monitor) by executives.
questions.pre_read: Recall COBIT's governance domain and its four management domains. Ask which body sets direction and which executes.
questions.correct_explanation: COBIT 2019 assigns governance to the board through the Evaluate, Direct and Monitor domain, while executive management plans, builds, runs and monitors through the four management domains. Approving each project's design is tempting because it sounds like strong oversight, but it pulls the board into management detail; the board directs priorities and monitors results rather than designing projects.

wrong_explanations.A: Approving project design and schedules is management work. The board sets direction and monitors outcomes across the portfolio.
wrong_explanations.C: COBIT deliberately separates governance from management. Identical accountabilities would blur who directs and who executes.
wrong_explanations.D: This inverts the roles: boards do not operate IT, and management does more than review annually.

tips: Eliminate: C erases the governance and management split, and D inverts the two roles.
Final two: B beats A because the board directs and monitors; approving project design is management detail.
Exam cue: board = Evaluate, Direct, Monitor; management = Plan, Build, Run, Monitor.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 (Governance vs Management); ISO/IEC 38500:2015 Information technology - Governance of IT for the organization
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Senior Mgmt and Boards IT governance roles - COBIT 2019 EDM (board) vs APO/BAI/DSS/MEA (management) split, distinct from d2_006 (InfoSec governance board accountability)'. Public source: COBIT 2019. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.subtopic: IT Org Structure. RACI / Function Design
questions.question: An IS auditor reviews a logistics company's RACI chart for its IT functions. Which design feature MOST strongly supports clear accountability?

options.A: Every IT staff member reporting directly to the CIO
options.B: Reorganizing IT functions each quarter to match priorities
options.C: A single Accountable role assigned to each outcome
options.D: Two Accountable roles assigned to each critical outcome

questions.key_concept: RACI design names one Accountable role per outcome; several Accountable roles dilute ownership and let decisions fall between them.
questions.pre_read: Recall what the A in RACI means. Ask what happens when two people both own the same result.
questions.correct_explanation: Clear accountability means one role answers for each outcome, with Responsible, Consulted and Informed roles around it. Two Accountable roles can look more rigorous for critical outcomes, but in practice each assumes the other is in charge, decisions stall and failures have no clear owner. The fix for criticality is stronger oversight, not shared accountability.

wrong_explanations.A: A flat structure overloads the CIO and does not scale. It does not define who is accountable for each outcome.
wrong_explanations.B: Frequent reorganizations make roles unstable, so accountability keeps shifting and becomes harder to trace.
wrong_explanations.D: Two Accountable roles dilute ownership. Each can defer to the other, so no one clearly answers for the outcome.

tips: Eliminate: A overloads one executive, and B keeps roles unstable; neither defines outcome ownership.
Final two: C beats D because one Accountable per outcome keeps ownership clear; two owners dilute it.
Exam cue: in RACI questions, many can be Responsible, but only one can be Accountable.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 APO01 (Managed I&T Management Framework)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'IT Org Structure RACI design - singular Accountable principle, distinct from d2_008 (SoD toxic combination identification)'. Public source: COBIT 2019 APO01. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: An IS auditor reviews network management at a hospital network. Which control set BEST supports network governance?

options.A: A firewall rule document last updated three years ago
options.B: Reliance on senior engineers' knowledge of the environment
options.C: Real-time traffic dashboards from a central network tool
options.D: Documented segmentation with managed rule changes and flow reviews

questions.key_concept: Network governance needs documented architecture and segmentation, change control over rule sets and periodic review of allowed traffic flows.
questions.pre_read: Ask which option shows the network is designed, changed and reviewed under control, not just watched.
questions.correct_explanation: Governance requires the network to be designed on purpose, changed under control and reviewed regularly. Documented segmentation, managed changes to firewall and access rules, and periodic flow reviews provide that, along with audit evidence. Monitoring dashboards are useful detective tools, but they show traffic, not whether rules are authorized, documented or still needed.

wrong_explanations.A: A three-year-old document with no change tracking cannot show what rules are in place today or why.
wrong_explanations.B: Unwritten knowledge cannot be audited and leaves with the people who hold it.
wrong_explanations.C: Dashboards detect activity but do not show that rules were authorized, documented and reviewed.

tips: Eliminate: A is stale documentation, and B is unwritten knowledge that cannot be audited.
Final two: D beats C because governance needs authorized design and change control; monitoring only observes traffic.
Exam cue: governance answers show designed, controlled and reviewed; monitoring alone is detective, not governance.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 DSS05 (Managed Security Services); ISACA Network Perimeter Security Audit/Assurance Program
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Network Management governance and audit - architecture + change mgmt + baselines + flow review, no prior question on this 2.2.8 sub-bullet'. Public source: COBIT 2019 DSS05. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: An IT risk manager has reliable loss data for some IT risks but only expert judgment for others. Which analysis method is MOST appropriate?

options.A: Semi-quantitative scores on calibrated scales with value bands
options.B: Qualitative high, medium and low ratings applied to every risk
options.C: Monte Carlo simulation for every risk regardless of available data
options.D: Business unit intuition without a formal analysis method

questions.key_concept: Semi-quantitative analysis uses calibrated scales so loss data and expert judgment can be compared consistently across a mixed evidence base.
questions.pre_read: Notice the evidence is mixed. Ask which method uses the data where it exists without inventing it where it does not.
questions.correct_explanation: Calibrated scales with defined value bands let the manager score data-rich risks precisely and judgment-based risks consistently, so all risks can be ranked on one basis. Qualitative ratings are tempting because they work everywhere, but they discard the precision the loss data offers and make rankings depend more on individual interpretation.

wrong_explanations.B: Pure qualitative ratings ignore the available loss data and rely on subjective labels that different raters read differently.
wrong_explanations.C: Simulation without data produces precise-looking numbers built on guesses, giving false confidence.
wrong_explanations.D: Intuition without a method cannot be repeated, compared or defended to management and the board.

tips: Eliminate: C invents precision where no data exists, and D abandons a repeatable method.
Final two: A beats B because calibrated scales keep the loss data's precision; plain ratings throw it away.
Exam cue: data everywhere → quantitative; data nowhere → qualitative; mixed evidence → semi-quantitative.
questions.framework_ref: IEC 31010:2019 (Risk Assessment Techniques); ISACA Risk IT Framework; COBIT 2019 APO12 (Managed Risk)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Risk Analysis semi-quantitative method - mixed-evidence fit, distinct from d2_012 (qualitative vs quantitative selection at higher level)'. Public source: ISO 31010:2019. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: An IS auditor reviews a health-tech firm's new privacy program after the policy is approved. Which rollout approach BEST supports sustained operation?

options.A: Publishing the approved policy on the intranet for staff
options.B: Timing the rollout to the next regulatory examination cycle
options.C: Embedding privacy tasks into existing processes with unit stewards
options.D: Centralizing privacy enforcement and accountability in the DPO's team

questions.key_concept: Privacy programs last when controls are built into existing processes and business units have named privacy stewards.
questions.pre_read: Ask who handles personal data every day. Sustained privacy depends on them, not on a policy document.
questions.correct_explanation: Privacy is sustained when it runs inside normal work: data subject requests in ticketing, breaches in incident response, records of processing in change management, with named stewards in each business unit. Centralizing enforcement with the data protection officer is tempting, but the officer oversees and advises; the business units that process personal data must own day-to-day compliance.

wrong_explanations.A: Publishing a policy creates awareness at best. Without process integration or training, behavior rarely changes.
wrong_explanations.B: Pacing work to examinations makes compliance reactive and leaves personal data exposed until the regulator arrives.
wrong_explanations.D: A central team cannot see every process. Accountability must sit with the units that handle the data, with the officer overseeing.

tips: Eliminate: A stops at publication, and B paces privacy work to the regulator instead of the risk.
Final two: C beats D because the data protection officer oversees; business units handling the data own daily compliance.
Exam cue: sustainable programs are embedded in existing processes with local accountability, not run by one central function.
questions.framework_ref: NIST Privacy Framework v1.0; ISO/IEC 27701:2019 (Privacy Information Management); GDPR Article 24 (Controller Responsibility)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Privacy Program rollout/operationalization - embedded controls + stewards, distinct from d2_013 (privacy program 8-element design) and d2_029 (multi-regulation privacy audit)'. Public source: ISACA Privacy Program guidance + IAPP. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: A retailer's chief information security officer reviews how the security program runs after its initial design. Which practice MOST strongly sustains the program's effectiveness?

options.A: An annual ISMS internal audit run separately from daily operations
options.B: Quarterly penetration tests filed as compliance evidence
options.C: Working the security backlog when incidents reveal gaps
options.D: A monthly risk review fed by incidents and control indicators

questions.key_concept: Security programs stay effective through an integrated cadence: risk reviews fed by incidents and control indicators, reported to leadership and informing audits.
questions.pre_read: Look for the option that links incidents, metrics and risk decisions into one recurring cycle.
questions.correct_explanation: A monthly risk review that takes in incidents and control indicators keeps the risk register current and turns what the team learns into treatment decisions. The annual ISMS internal audit is required under ISO/IEC 27001 and is tempting, but run in isolation it gives a yearly snapshot rather than the continuous feedback that sustains effectiveness.

wrong_explanations.A: An isolated annual audit gives periodic assurance but does not feed incidents and metrics into risk decisions during the year.
wrong_explanations.B: Test findings filed for compliance never reach the risk treatment plan, so weaknesses persist.
wrong_explanations.C: Waiting for incidents makes the program reactive and lets known weaknesses remain until they are exploited.

tips: Eliminate: B files findings without acting on them, and C waits for incidents to drive work.
Final two: D beats A because a recurring risk cycle drives decisions all year; an isolated annual audit is a snapshot.
Exam cue: sustained effectiveness means a feedback loop; incidents and metrics should change risk decisions.
questions.framework_ref: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 (Information Security Management Systems); ISACA Information Security Management Audit/Assurance Program; COBIT 2019 APO13 (Managed Security)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'InfoSec Mgmt operational running - integrated cadence, distinct from d2_025 (8-element program structure) and d2_006 (board accountability)'. Public source: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 + ISACA InfoSec Mgmt guidance. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: A logistics company's IT teams use ITIL 4, SAFe and ISO 9001, and the CEO wants operational excellence. Which approach should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Adopt Lean as the single operational excellence method for every team
options.B: Keep the current frameworks, linked by shared excellence goals and metrics
options.C: Defer the initiative until each framework matures separately
options.D: Replace the frameworks immediately with one CEO-selected model

questions.key_concept: Operational excellence in mixed IT environments links fitting frameworks through shared goals and metrics rather than forcing a single method.
questions.pre_read: Notice each framework already serves a different team. Ask how to point them at one goal without losing fit.
questions.correct_explanation: Each framework fits its domain: ITIL 4 for service management, SAFe for delivery, ISO 9001 for regulated quality. Keeping them, linked by shared cost, quality and speed goals and metrics, preserves that fit, with Lean or Six Sigma applied where they fit. Adopting Lean everywhere is tempting for consistency, but it discards domain fit, including the regulated group's quality discipline.

wrong_explanations.A: A single method across every team ignores domain needs and could weaken the regulated group's established quality system.
wrong_explanations.C: Waiting for separate maturity keeps teams pulling in different directions and delays the business goal.
wrong_explanations.D: Abrupt replacement disrupts working practices and regulated processes, with no evidence the new model fits each domain.

tips: Eliminate: C delays the business goal indefinitely, and D forces disruptive replacement of working practices.
Final two: B beats A because linking the fitting frameworks through shared goals keeps domain strengths; one method everywhere discards them.
Exam cue: when several frameworks each fit their area, choose integration under governance over replacement or uniformity.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 APO11 (Managed Quality); EFQM Model (2020); ITIL 4; ISO 9001:2015
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Operational Excellence framework selection - layered strategy distinct from d2_048 (Quality Mgmt framework selection at smaller scale) and d2_028 (Six Sigma/Agile/BSC method-fit selection)'. Public source: ISACA OpEx + EFQM Model 2020. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: A SaaS company's privacy team runs separate processes for 14 privacy laws and is overwhelmed by exceptions. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: A global baseline with mapped jurisdiction-specific exceptions
options.B: Applying GDPR uniformly worldwide as the strictest privacy regime
options.C: Applying the most permissive privacy law uniformly worldwide
options.D: Building a separate privacy program for each jurisdiction

questions.key_concept: Multi-jurisdiction privacy scales through a global baseline of common requirements plus a mapped exception layer for local rules.
questions.pre_read: Notice the team is already overwhelmed by separate processes. Ask which design reduces duplication without missing local rules.
questions.correct_explanation: A global baseline covers what most laws share, such as data subject rights, breach notification and retention, while a control library maps local exceptions. Applying GDPR everywhere is tempting because it is demanding, but no single law is strictest on every point; local rules on consent, localization or notification timing would still be missed.

wrong_explanations.B: GDPR is not the strictest law on every requirement. Some jurisdictions add rules it lacks, so gaps remain.
wrong_explanations.C: Adopting the weakest standard invites enforcement wherever stricter laws apply.
wrong_explanations.D: Separate programs are the current problem. They multiply duplicated work and do not scale.

tips: Eliminate: C invites enforcement, and D repeats the siloed approach that is already failing.
Final two: A beats B because no single law is strictest everywhere; a baseline plus mapped exceptions covers local rules.
Exam cue: for many overlapping regulations, prefer one common baseline with mapped exceptions over silos or a single law.
questions.framework_ref: ISO/IEC 27701:2019 (Privacy Information Management); NIST Privacy Framework v1.0; GDPR; CCPA/CPRA; LGPD; PIPL; PIPEDA; UK-GDPR

questions.subtopic: Cloud Migration Risk. Lift-and-Shift vs Refactor
questions.question: A manufacturer's 80-application portfolio mixes stable legacy, fast-changing, vendor-managed and retirement-candidate systems. What should the IS auditor recommend as the BEST cloud migration approach?

options.A: Rehost every application in one board-approved lift-and-shift wave
options.B: Refactor every application to be cloud-native before moving
options.C: Delay migration until cloud practices mature across the industry
options.D: Choose to retire, rehost, refactor or repurchase per application

questions.key_concept: Heterogeneous portfolios need a per-application migration decision (retire, retain, rehost, replatform, refactor, repurchase) based on value and risk.
questions.pre_read: Notice the portfolio has four different kinds of systems. Ask whether one strategy can suit all of them.
questions.correct_explanation: Different systems carry different value and risk, so each needs its own decision: retire candidates first to shrink scope, rehost stable legacy systems, refactor fast-changing ones and replace vendor products with SaaS. A single board-approved lift-and-shift wave is tempting for its simplicity, but it moves retirement candidates at cost and leaves high-value systems without cloud benefits.

wrong_explanations.A: Board approval does not fix uniform rehosting, which migrates systems that should be retired and forgoes value where refactoring would pay off.
wrong_explanations.B: Refactoring everything spends heavily on stable or retiring systems and stretches the timeline for little benefit.
wrong_explanations.C: Indefinite delay avoids the decision and leaves the business case and current risks unaddressed.

tips: Eliminate: B overspends on systems that do not need refactoring, and C avoids the decision.
Final two: D beats A because each system's value and risk differ; uniform rehosting even migrates retirement candidates.
Exam cue: a mixed portfolio calls for per-item decisions; one-size-fits-all strategies are usually distractors.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Cloud Computing Management Audit/Assurance Program; COBIT 2019 APO05 (Managed Portfolio); Microsoft Cloud Adoption Framework for Azure; AWS Prescriptive Guidance: Migration Strategies
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Cloud Migration Risk - 6 Rs framework for heterogeneous portfolios, distinct from d2_014 (shared responsibility) and d2_017 (outsourcing decision multi-factor)'. Public source: ISACA Cloud Computing + Gartner. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: Mid-year, a retailer's board mandates a 12% IT budget cut while a new PCI DSS deadline adds unplanned spend. What should the IS auditor recommend as the BEST response?

options.A: Cut run, grow and transform budgets by the same percentage
options.B: Cut run spending to fund the PCI DSS compliance work
options.C: Re-rank portfolio items by risk and value for board reauthorization
options.D: Let the CIO shift funds across categories without board review

questions.key_concept: Material mid-year portfolio changes need risk- and value-based reprioritization, then reauthorization by the body that approved the original portfolio.
questions.pre_read: Recall who approved the original portfolio. Ask who must approve a material change to it.
questions.correct_explanation: Re-ranking items by risk and value protects lights-on and compliance spend while cutting where near-term risk is lowest, and board reauthorization keeps the governing body accountable for the revised plan. Letting the CIO reallocate is tempting because it is fast, but the board approved the original allocation, so a material change made under existing authority bypasses governance.

wrong_explanations.A: Equal cuts ignore priorities and can starve run operations or the compliance work as much as optional projects.
wrong_explanations.B: Cutting run spending threatens system stability and the operations the business depends on today.
wrong_explanations.D: A material change to a board-approved portfolio needs board reauthorization, not a unilateral management decision.

tips: Eliminate: A ignores priority, and B endangers the operations that keep the business running.
Final two: C beats D because the board approved the portfolio; material changes need its reauthorization, not CIO discretion.
Exam cue: when approved plans change materially, the answer returns the decision to the body that approved them.

questions.subtopic: InfoSec Governance. EGIT / Risk / Quality Integration
questions.question: A hospital board receives conflicting IT reports from separate IT governance, enterprise risk and information security committees. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Fold the three bodies into the information security committee
options.B: Integrate agendas, scorecards and registers, keeping decision rights
options.C: Add a fourth governance committee to reconcile the others
options.D: Disband the two weakest committees whatever coverage is lost

questions.key_concept: Overlapping governance bodies should share an integrated agenda, scorecard and risk register while each keeps its distinct decision rights.
questions.pre_read: Notice the problem is contradictory reporting, not too few committees. Ask what gives the board one consistent view.
questions.correct_explanation: The board's problem is three inconsistent views of IT. Integrating agendas, scorecards and risk registers gives one consistent picture while each body keeps its own decision rights. A fourth governance committee is tempting because it leaves existing structures intact, but it adds a layer that reconciles conflicting data after the fact instead of removing the cause.

wrong_explanations.A: Folding everything into security lets one domain dominate and loses enterprise risk and broader IT governance coverage.
wrong_explanations.C: Another committee adds overhead and reconciles conflicting outputs afterward; the separate scorecards and registers remain.
wrong_explanations.D: Disbanding committees regardless of coverage leaves governance gaps the board would not see.

tips: Eliminate: A lets one domain take over, and D accepts lost governance coverage.
Final two: B beats C because integration removes the conflicting data at source; a fourth committee just reconciles it later.
Exam cue: fix fragmented governance by integrating information and cadence, not by adding layers or deleting oversight.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 EDM03 (Ensured Risk Optimization); ISACA Information Security Management Audit/Assurance Program; ISO/IEC 27014 (Governance of Information Security)

questions.question: A bank's core banking middleware has a high-likelihood, high-impact risk, and the vendor will issue no further patches. Which risk treatment should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Upgrade or replace the middleware to remove the exposure
options.B: Accept the risk with documented sign-off from the board
options.C: Transfer the risk by purchasing a cyber insurance policy
options.D: Add the risk to the register for annual review

questions.key_concept: Treatment must match the risk: high-likelihood, high-impact exposures with no vendor fix call for mitigation or avoidance, not acceptance or transfer alone.
questions.pre_read: Notice both ratings are high and no patch is coming. Ask which treatment actually reduces likelihood or impact.
questions.correct_explanation: A high-likelihood, high-impact risk almost certainly exceeds appetite, and no patch will reduce it, so the bank should mitigate or avoid it by upgrading or replacing the product. Insurance is tempting because it limits financial loss, but it leaves the vulnerability in place; service outages, customer harm and regulatory consequences remain with the bank.

wrong_explanations.B: Acceptance suits risks within appetite. A high-likelihood, high-impact unpatched exposure in core banking is unlikely to qualify.
wrong_explanations.C: Insurance offsets some financial loss but leaves the vulnerability exploitable and the operational and regulatory impact unchanged.
wrong_explanations.D: Recording the risk for later review is monitoring, not treatment, and leaves a known exposure in place for a year.

tips: Eliminate: B accepts a risk far beyond appetite, and D only records it without treating it.
Final two: A beats C because insurance leaves the vulnerability in place; mitigation reduces the risk itself.
Exam cue: high likelihood plus high impact points to reduce or avoid; transfer only covers part of the financial loss.
questions.framework_ref: ISO 31000:2018 (Risk Management); ISACA Risk IT Framework; COSO ERM (2017); COBIT 2019 APO12 (Managed Risk)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Risk Treatment multi-option application scenario - per-risk treatment matching, distinct from d2_022 (foundational treatment options definition) and d2_007 (risk lifecycle gap analysis)'. Public source: ISO 31000:2018 + ISACA Risk IT. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: An IS auditor maps roles to the IIA Three Lines Model. Which line BEST describes a compliance function that monitors IT risk managed by operations?

options.A: First line, because it manages risk within daily operations
options.B: Second line, providing risk expertise, monitoring and challenge
options.C: Third line, because it reports independently to the board
options.D: Outside the model, because it sits apart from operations and audit

questions.key_concept: In the IIA Three Lines Model, operations owns risk, risk and compliance functions support and challenge, and internal audit independently assures.
questions.pre_read: Separate who owns the risk, who supports and challenges, and who is fully independent of management.
questions.correct_explanation: Compliance supports and challenges how operations manages risk, which is the second-line role in the IIA Three Lines Model. Third line is tempting because compliance may report to the board, but the third line is internal audit, which provides assurance fully independent of management; compliance remains part of management's structure.

wrong_explanations.A: The first line is operations itself, which owns and manages the risk. Compliance monitors that work rather than doing it.
wrong_explanations.C: The third line is internal audit, independent of management. Board reporting alone does not give compliance that independence.
wrong_explanations.D: Second-line functions are part of the model and do provide assurance to management and the governing body.

tips: Eliminate: A describes operations itself, and D wrongly places compliance outside the model.
Final two: B beats C because independence from management defines the third line; compliance remains a management function.
Exam cue: own the risk = first line; support and challenge = second line; independent assurance = internal audit.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds several regional hospitals sharing a cloud built for their common regulatory needs. Which NIST SP 800-145 deployment model BEST describes this arrangement?

options.A: Private cloud
options.B: Community cloud
options.C: Hybrid cloud
options.D: Public cloud

questions.key_concept: NIST deployment models differ by who uses the infrastructure: public (general public), private (one organization), community (organizations with shared concerns), hybrid (combination).
questions.pre_read: Ask how many organizations use the cloud and what ties them together.
questions.correct_explanation: NIST SP 800-145 defines a community cloud as infrastructure provisioned for exclusive use by a specific community of organizations with shared concerns, such as regulatory requirements. Private cloud is tempting because access is restricted, but private infrastructure serves a single organization, and here several separate hospitals share it.

wrong_explanations.A: A private cloud serves one organization. Several separate hospitals sharing the infrastructure goes beyond that definition.
wrong_explanations.C: A hybrid cloud combines two or more distinct deployment models. Nothing here describes such a combination.
wrong_explanations.D: A public cloud is open to the general public. This one is restricted to hospitals with common concerns.

tips: Eliminate: C needs two combined models, and D is open to the general public.
Final two: B beats A because several organizations share it; private cloud serves exactly one.
Exam cue: count the organizations: one = private; a group with shared concerns = community; anyone = public.

questions.question: A data governance committee is defining enterprise data classification levels. Which basis for the levels is MOST appropriate?

options.A: Impact on the organization if data is disclosed or altered
options.B: Regulatory category of the data, such as personal or financial
options.C: Lifecycle stage of the data, such as active or archived
options.D: Storage location of the data, such as cloud or on-premises

questions.key_concept: Classification levels grade data by the harm its disclosure or alteration would cause, so each level carries matching handling and protection rules.
questions.pre_read: Ask what classification is for: deciding how strongly to protect data. Pick the basis that measures harm.
questions.correct_explanation: Classification exists to set protection in proportion to risk, so levels such as public, internal, confidential and restricted are graded by the impact of disclosure or alteration. Handling, access and encryption rules then follow each level. Regulatory category is a useful input, but data within one category, such as personal data, can range from low to severe impact.

wrong_explanations.B: Category describes subject matter, not sensitivity. Personal or financial data can sit at different levels depending on the harm its disclosure would cause.
wrong_explanations.C: Lifecycle stage says where data is in its life, not how sensitive it is. Archived records can still be highly restricted.
wrong_explanations.D: Storage location is a deployment fact. The same data needs the same protection wherever it is held.

tips: Eliminate: C describes lifecycle stage and D describes storage location; neither measures how sensitive the data is.
Final two: A beats B because classification is risk-based; one regulatory category can hold data of very different impact.
Exam cue: when asked how to classify data, choose the option based on impact or sensitivity, not on topic, age or place.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 APO14 (Managed Data); NIST SP 800-60; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 (Information Security Management Systems)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Data Classification foundational - 4-tier sensitivity model, complements d2_016 (application - classification approach in regulated context)'. Public source: ISACA Data Governance + NIST SP 800-60. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: An IS auditor is mapping a client's control documentation to the COSO Internal Control–Integrated Framework (2013). Which set of components is MOST appropriate for the mapping?

options.A: Identify, protect, detect, respond, and recover security functions
options.B: Plan, do, check, and act improvement cycles for control
options.C: Control environment, risk assessment, control activities, information and communication, monitoring activities
options.D: Internal environment, objective setting, event identification, risk response, and monitoring activities

questions.key_concept: COSO 2013 has five integrated internal control components: control environment, risk assessment, control activities, information and communication, and monitoring activities.
questions.pre_read: Check which framework each list comes from. Two lists belong to other models, and one borrows terms from COSO's risk work.
questions.correct_explanation: The COSO Internal Control–Integrated Framework (2013) defines five integrated components: control environment, risk assessment, control activities, information and communication, and monitoring activities, supported by 17 principles. Mapping to these lets the auditor see gaps by component. The runner-up mixes in objective setting, event identification and risk response, which come from the 2004 COSO enterprise risk management cube, not the internal control framework.

wrong_explanations.A: These are the core functions of the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, a security model rather than COSO internal control.
wrong_explanations.B: Plan-do-check-act is the Deming improvement cycle used in management systems such as ISO standards, not COSO components.
wrong_explanations.D: Objective setting, event identification and risk response belong to the 2004 COSO ERM model, so this list does not match the 2013 framework.

tips: Eliminate: A is the NIST Cybersecurity Framework and B is the Deming improvement cycle; neither is COSO.
Final two: C beats D because D mixes in enterprise risk management components that the internal control framework does not use.
Exam cue: for COSO internal control, remember the five components start with control environment and end with monitoring activities.

questions.question: An IS auditor reviews how the CIO reports IT's value to the board. Which measure BEST demonstrates the value delivered by IT?

options.A: Annual IT budget and headcount compared with industry peers
options.B: Number of help-desk tickets resolved within service targets
options.C: Projects delivered on schedule and within their approved budgets
options.D: Realized business benefits traced to approved IT investments

questions.key_concept: IT value is shown by business outcomes realized from IT-enabled investments, not by inputs, activity counts or delivery performance.
questions.pre_read: Separate what IT spends and does from what the business gains. The board cares about outcomes.
questions.correct_explanation: Under COBIT 2019 EDM02, value means business benefits realized from IT-enabled investments, such as revenue enabled, cost avoided or risk reduced, traced back to the business case. That is outcome evidence the board can act on. On-time, on-budget delivery shows good project execution, but a project can be delivered perfectly and still produce no business benefit.

wrong_explanations.A: Budget and headcount are inputs. Spending more than peers says nothing about what the business gained.
wrong_explanations.B: Ticket counts measure operational activity. They show IT is busy, not that it creates business value.
wrong_explanations.C: Delivery on schedule and budget measures project execution. A well-run project can still fail to deliver the expected benefits.

tips: Eliminate: A measures inputs and B counts activity; neither links IT to a business result.
Final two: D beats C because benefits delivery is judged by outcomes realized, not by how well the project was run.
Exam cue: when the question is about IT value, pick the outcome tied to business objectives over inputs, outputs or activity.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 EDM02 (Ensured Benefits Delivery); COBIT 2019 APO05 (Managed Portfolio)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Value of IT (2.8.1) - outcome-based quantification, distinct from input/activity/perception metrics'. Public source: COBIT 2019 EDM02. questions.question: A healthcare technology firm is building its first enterprise data inventory. Which approach should the IS auditor recommend as MOST sustainable over time?

options.A: A one-time survey asking each department to list its data
options.B: Named data stewards recording new assets through change management
options.C: Quarterly automated discovery scans run by the security team
options.D: The IT asset database, inferring data from systems recorded

questions.key_concept: A data inventory stays current when named stewards capture new data assets as part of normal change processes, not as a separate exercise.
questions.pre_read: Sustainable means the inventory updates itself as the business changes. Look for ownership built into an existing process.
questions.correct_explanation: A sustainable inventory needs accountability and a trigger. Named data stewards, working through change management, record each new data asset at creation, with its purpose and sensitivity. The inventory then grows with the business. Automated discovery scans are valuable for finding unknown data, but they run on a schedule, lack business context such as purpose and owner, and do not make anyone accountable.

wrong_explanations.A: A one-time survey is out of date as soon as it is finished, and depends on staff remembering every data store.
wrong_explanations.C: Scans find data stores but miss business context such as purpose and ownership, and they leave gaps between quarterly runs.
wrong_explanations.D: An IT asset database lists hardware and software. It does not show what data those systems hold or who owns it.

tips: Eliminate: A is a one-off snapshot and D tracks systems, not the data inside them.
Final two: B beats C because named stewards capture assets at creation, while scans only find data later and without business context.
Exam cue: for anything meant to stay current, prefer named ownership built into an existing process over a periodic sweep.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 APO14 (Managed Data); DAMA-DMBOK 2nd Edition
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Data Inventory (2.7.1 depth) - sustainable methodology with discovery + stewardship + change integration, distinct from d2_016 (classification approach)'. Public source: ISACA Data Governance + DAMA-DMBOK. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: An IS auditor reviews governance over a manufacturer's 40 concurrent IT projects. Which arrangement BEST supports oversight at portfolio level?

options.A: A PMO applying standard stage gates and consolidated reporting
options.B: A separate steering committee providing oversight for each project
options.C: Informal email updates sent at each project manager's discretion
options.D: Rotating project slots on an existing operational status meeting

questions.key_concept: Portfolio-scale oversight needs a PMO with a common method, stage gates and consolidated reporting so leaders can compare and prioritize projects.
questions.pre_read: Note the scale: 40 projects at once. Ask which option lets leaders see across projects, not just into one.
questions.correct_explanation: With 40 projects, leadership must compare progress, risks, dependencies and resources across the whole portfolio. A PMO applying a standard method, stage gates and consolidated reporting gives that view and consistent escalation. Per-project steering committees give each project clear oversight, but each sees only its own project, so conflicts over resources and priorities across the portfolio go unmanaged.

wrong_explanations.B: Per-project committees provide accountability, but no one sees across projects to resolve shared resource conflicts or reprioritize the portfolio.
wrong_explanations.C: Informal, irregular updates give no consistent data and no basis for escalation or comparison across projects.
wrong_explanations.D: Ad hoc slots in an operational meeting give partial, uneven coverage and no structured gate decisions.

tips: Eliminate: C has no standard cadence and D gives random, partial coverage.
Final two: A beats B because portfolio oversight needs one consolidated view, while per-project committees each see only their own project.
Exam cue: when the stem stresses many projects, choose the option that gives a portfolio view, not stronger single-project control.

questions.question: An IS auditor assesses a bank's IT delivery against COBIT 2019 APO11 (Managed Quality). Which practice is MOST consistent with this objective?

options.A: A quality manager personally approving every release
options.B: Quarterly business satisfaction surveys used as the quality measure
options.C: Defined quality standards plus metrics-driven root-cause improvement
options.D: Quality assurance outsourced, with no internal quality standards

questions.key_concept: APO11 builds quality into processes through defined standards, integrated assurance, measurement and continuous improvement, rather than relying on final inspection.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether quality is designed into the process or checked at the end by one person.
questions.correct_explanation: APO11 expects a quality management system: defined standards and acceptance criteria, quality activities built into delivery, measurement, and continuous improvement from root-cause analysis. Quality then improves at the source. A manager approving every release adds a final check, but it relies on one person, becomes a bottleneck, and catches defects late instead of preventing them.

wrong_explanations.A: One person inspecting every release is a late, single-point check. It does not set standards or fix causes.
wrong_explanations.B: Satisfaction surveys are lagging, perception-based signals. They miss process measures and defect prevention.
wrong_explanations.D: Outsourcing assurance without internal standards leaves the bank unable to define or judge the quality it needs.

tips: Eliminate: B relies on lagging perception data and D leaves the bank with no quality standards of its own.
Final two: C beats A because APO11 builds quality into the process, while a personal gatekeeper only inspects at the end.
Exam cue: for quality questions, prefer standards, measurement and root-cause improvement over end-of-line inspection by one person.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 APO11 (Managed Quality); ISO 9001:2015
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'APO11 Quality Management application - 4 practice areas, complementing d2_020 (QA program effectiveness analysis) and d2_048 (quality framework selection analysis)'. questions.question: An IS auditor reviews a draft SLA with a new cloud infrastructure provider. Which clause MOST strongly protects the customer's interests?

options.A: Best-effort language preserving flexibility for both parties
options.B: Targets defined and reported by the provider's standard tooling
options.C: A 99.99 percent availability target stated in the contract
options.D: Measurable targets backed by service credits and exit rights

questions.key_concept: An SLA protects the customer only when targets are measurable and backed by consequences such as service credits and exit rights.
questions.pre_read: A high number in a contract is not leverage by itself. Ask what happens when the provider misses it.
questions.correct_explanation: An SLA protects the customer when targets are measurable, the measurement method is defined, and misses have consequences: service credits for breaches and exit rights for sustained underperformance. That gives the customer enforceable leverage. A 99.99 percent availability target sounds strong, but without a defined measurement method and remedies the provider faces no cost for missing it.

wrong_explanations.A: Best-effort wording sets no enforceable standard, so the customer has no basis to claim a breach.
wrong_explanations.B: Provider-defined targets and reporting let the provider mark its own work, removing independent verification.
wrong_explanations.C: A high target with no measurement method or remedy gives the customer nothing to enforce when service falls short.

tips: Eliminate: A sets no enforceable standard and B lets the provider define and grade its own performance.
Final two: D beats C because a target only protects the customer when misses carry consequences such as credits or exit.
Exam cue: in contract questions, enforceability beats ambition; look for measurement plus remedies.

Public source: COBIT 2019 APO09. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: An IS auditor reviews a cyber risk analysis that claims to follow the FAIR model. Which inputs BEST show that the analysis truly applies FAIR?

options.A: Qualitative high, medium and low ratings averaged into a heat map
options.B: Loss event frequency and loss magnitude, each expressed as ranges
options.C: Single loss expectancy multiplied by its annualized rate of occurrence
options.D: Pass or fail judgments on each control, totalled into a score

questions.key_concept: FAIR decomposes risk into loss event frequency and loss magnitude, estimated as ranges and simulated to give a distribution of annual loss.
questions.pre_read: Both quantitative options use numbers. Ask which one decomposes risk and shows uncertainty rather than a single figure.
questions.correct_explanation: FAIR breaks risk into loss event frequency, driven by threat event frequency and vulnerability, and loss magnitude, made up of primary and secondary loss. Each factor is estimated as a calibrated range and simulated, usually with Monte Carlo, to give a range of annual loss. Classic ALE is quantitative too, but it multiplies two point estimates and hides both the drivers and the uncertainty.

wrong_explanations.A: Averaged qualitative ratings are not quantitative and cannot express loss in money or probability.
wrong_explanations.C: This is the classic ALE formula. It gives one point estimate and does not decompose frequency or magnitude drivers.
wrong_explanations.D: Counting failing controls measures control status, not how often losses occur or how large they are.

tips: Eliminate: A is qualitative scoring and D counts control failures; neither estimates loss.
Final two: B beats C because FAIR decomposes frequency and magnitude and uses ranges, while ALE multiplies two single-point guesses.
Exam cue: FAIR means frequency times magnitude, expressed as distributions; a single number signals classic ALE, not FAIR.

questions.question: A bank's IT steering committee wants to trial generative AI without weakening IT discipline. Which approach BEST meets this goal?

options.A: Sandboxed pilots with stage gates into standard IT processes
options.B: A separate innovation lab kept fully isolated from production IT
options.C: Open experimentation by any team without governance review
options.D: Waiting until peers have used the technology for three years

questions.key_concept: Managed innovation lets ideas be tested safely and then move through defined gates into normal governance once they prove value.
questions.pre_read: The goal has two halves: innovate and keep discipline. Pick the option that achieves both, not just one.
questions.correct_explanation: COBIT 2019 APO04 supports innovation that serves business goals under control. Sandboxes contain the risk of experiments, defined criteria and stage gates decide what moves from experiment to pilot to production, and successful ideas then join standard governance. An isolated lab also protects production, but with no path into it, good ideas never reach the business and benefits are not delivered.

wrong_explanations.B: Isolation protects production, but without a route into standard governance good experiments stall and deliver no business value.
wrong_explanations.C: Ungoverned experimentation exposes the bank to data, security and compliance risk with no evaluation criteria.
wrong_explanations.D: A blanket wait forfeits competitive value and replaces risk management with avoidance.

tips: Eliminate: C drops discipline entirely and D drops innovation entirely.
Final two: A beats B because stage gates create a governed path to production, while an isolated lab protects production but stalls value.
Exam cue: when a stem asks for innovation and control together, choose the staged, gated path over isolation or a ban.

First D2 question on innovation governance. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: An IS auditor reviews when an enterprise refreshes its IT strategy. Which approach BEST balances stability with responsiveness to change?

options.A: A refresh whenever a newly appointed CIO sets direction
options.B: A refresh whenever the external auditor recommends one
options.C: CIO-led updates each time a major technology shift reaches the market
options.D: Board-endorsed yearly reviews, updated for material business change

questions.key_concept: IT strategy should be reviewed on a regular cycle and updated when material business change occurs, with board endorsement of each revision.
questions.pre_read: Ask who should own strategy changes and what should trigger them: business change or technology events.
questions.correct_explanation: Under COBIT 2019 APO02, IT strategy follows enterprise strategy. A regular annual review gives stability, updates for material business change keep it responsive, and board endorsement keeps it aligned and owned by governance. CIO-led updates on technology shifts are responsive, but they let IT, not the business, set direction and bypass governance approval.

wrong_explanations.A: Tying strategy to leadership changes makes direction personal and unpredictable, not linked to business need.
wrong_explanations.B: The external auditor gives assurance, not direction. Strategy timing belongs to management and the board.
wrong_explanations.C: Technology-triggered updates owned by the CIO put IT ahead of business needs and skip board endorsement.

tips: Eliminate: A ties strategy to personnel changes and B hands strategy timing to an outside assurance provider.
Final two: D beats C because strategy must follow business change and be endorsed by governance, not be driven by IT events.
Exam cue: for IT strategy questions, prefer business-driven triggers and board ownership over IT-led or person-led change.

questions.question: An IS auditor reviews service agreements between a hospital's IT function and its business units. Which design BEST aligns with COBIT 2019 APO09?

options.A: Verbal agreements between IT directors and business unit heads
options.B: One standard SLA applied identically to every hospital business unit
options.C: Jointly agreed, documented service levels with regular performance reviews
options.D: Agreements drafted by IT and issued without business review

questions.key_concept: APO09 aligns IT services with business needs through agreed, documented service levels that are monitored and reviewed with each customer.
questions.pre_read: Business units differ in criticality. Ask which design lets each unit agree the service levels it needs.
questions.correct_explanation: COBIT 2019 APO09 expects service agreements that reflect each customer's needs, define service levels and responsibilities, and are monitored and reviewed regularly. Jointly agreed, documented service levels with regular performance reviews keep IT aligned to clinical and business priorities. One standard SLA is simpler and consistent, but it over-serves low-criticality units and under-serves critical ones such as clinical systems.

wrong_explanations.A: Verbal agreements leave no documented targets, so performance cannot be measured or disputes resolved.
wrong_explanations.B: A uniform SLA ignores differences in criticality and volume, so services are not aligned with each unit's needs.
wrong_explanations.D: IT-only drafting skips the customer, so agreed levels may not reflect what the business actually needs.

tips: Eliminate: A has nothing documented and D removes the business from the agreement.
Final two: C beats B because APO09 service levels are agreed with the customer and reviewed, while a uniform SLA is imposed and ignores criticality.
Exam cue: in service management questions, favour levels agreed with the customer, documented and reviewed regularly, over terms IT sets alone.

questions.question: Before a retailer deploys facial recognition for loss prevention, which privacy activity should management complete FIRST?

options.A: A vendor comparison based on cost and matching accuracy
options.B: A data protection impact assessment of the planned processing
options.C: Updated privacy notices informing shoppers about the cameras
options.D: A two-store pilot, with privacy review after value is proven

questions.key_concept: High-risk processing such as biometric identification requires a DPIA before it starts, to test necessity, proportionality and risks to individuals.
questions.pre_read: Biometric processing of the public is high risk. Ask what must be decided before anything else, including what to tell people.
questions.correct_explanation: GDPR Article 35 requires a data protection impact assessment before high-risk processing such as biometric identification. It describes the processing, tests necessity and proportionality, assesses risks to individuals and sets mitigations, and may show the plan should not go ahead. Updated notices are also required for transparency, but they inform people about processing that the DPIA must first show is justified.

wrong_explanations.A: Vendor cost and accuracy matter for procurement, but they do not assess necessity or risks to the people being scanned.
wrong_explanations.C: Notices are needed, but they only describe processing. The DPIA must first decide whether the processing is justified.
wrong_explanations.D: A pilot is itself live biometric processing of real shoppers, so the assessment must come before it, not after.

tips: Eliminate: A is a procurement step and D starts the risky processing before assessing it.
Final two: B beats C because the DPIA decides whether the processing should happen at all; notices only describe it.
Exam cue: for new high-risk processing, the impact assessment comes before deployment, notices and pilots.
questions.framework_ref: GDPR Article 35 (Data Protection Impact Assessment); Article 29 Working Party Guidelines on DPIA (WP248 rev.01, endorsed by the EDPB)
