questions.question: Fourteen months into a three-year IT strategy, a privacy law taking effect in nine months and a vendor end-of-support notice emerge. What should the IS auditor BEST recommend?

options.A: A focused, board-endorsed update addressing the material changes
options.B: Separate projects for each change, leaving the strategy as is
options.C: Replacing the strategy with a newly written three-year plan
options.D: Deferring the changes to the next annual strategy refresh

questions.key_concept: Material mid-cycle change calls for a focused, board-endorsed strategy update that keeps what still holds and re-aligns priorities and funding.
questions.pre_read: Weigh the size of the response against the size of the change, and ask who must approve shifts in direction.
questions.correct_explanation: Material changes mid-cycle mean the strategy's assumptions, priorities and funding no longer fully hold. A focused update addresses those changes, keeps the parts that remain valid, and goes to the board for endorsement so governance owns the revised direction. Separate projects respond quickly, but they shift resources and priorities outside the strategy, leaving the approved plan out of date.

wrong_explanations.B: Projects outside the strategy change priorities and funding without governance approval, so the approved plan no longer reflects reality.
wrong_explanations.C: Starting over discards still-valid work and causes churn. The changes call for an update, not a rewrite.
wrong_explanations.D: Waiting for the next refresh risks missing the privacy deadline and losing time to plan for vendor exit.

tips: Eliminate: C overreacts by discarding valid direction and D ignores the deadline already in view.
Final two: A beats B because changes to direction and funding need board endorsement, not workarounds outside the strategy.
Exam cue: when material change hits mid-cycle, choose a proportionate update approved by governance.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 APO02 (Managed Strategy); COBIT 2019 EDM01 (Ensured Governance Framework Setting and Maintenance)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'IT Strategy mid-cycle update analysis - focused update response to multiple material changes, distinct from d2_004/d2_024/d2_082 (other IT strategy angles)'. Public source: COBIT 2019 APO02. All scenario specifics (regional retailer, three triggers) invented for this question. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.subtopic: Privacy by Design vs Privacy by Default. Decision Synthesis
questions.question: A SaaS provider is adding an employee-analytics dashboard for its customers. Under GDPR Article 25, which default configuration should the IS auditor BEST recommend?

options.A: Full individual-level metrics, with an admin opt-out for each field
options.B: Pseudonymized individual-level metrics, with IP addresses still collected
options.C: Dashboard withheld from EU customers, full data shown elsewhere
options.D: Aggregated team metrics, individual views enabled for a stated purpose

questions.key_concept: Privacy by default means the out-of-the-box setting processes only the personal data needed, with more intrusive processing enabled deliberately for a defined purpose.
questions.pre_read: Focus on the word default. Ask which setting processes the least personal data before anyone changes anything.
questions.correct_explanation: GDPR Article 25 requires that, by default, only personal data necessary for each purpose is processed. Aggregated team metrics meet the analytics purpose without identifying individuals, and individual views are enabled only deliberately for a stated purpose. Pseudonymization is a useful design measure, but individual tracking with IP addresses is still personal data processed beyond what the default purpose needs.

wrong_explanations.A: An opt-out starts from maximum data collection, which is the opposite of protection by default.
wrong_explanations.B: Pseudonymized individual data with IP addresses is still personal data, and collecting it by default exceeds what is necessary.
wrong_explanations.C: Withholding the feature avoids rather than designs for privacy, and leaves employees elsewhere with no protection by default.

tips: Eliminate: A defaults to maximum collection and C avoids the design question instead of answering it.
Final two: D beats B because by default only necessary data is processed; pseudonymized individual tracking still exceeds that.
Exam cue: privacy by default means the least intrusive setting out of the box; opt-outs and partial masking fall short.
questions.framework_ref: GDPR Article 25 (Privacy by Design and Default); EDPB Guidelines 4/2019 (Article 25 Data Protection by Design and by Default); GDPR Article 13 (Information to be provided)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Privacy by Design vs Privacy by Default analysis - default-protective principle applied, distinct from d2_039/d2_040/d2_063/d2_066 (other privacy angles)'. Public source: GDPR Article 25 + EDPB 4/2019. All scenario specifics (SaaS platform employee analytics) invented for this question. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: A media company runs workloads on three cloud providers, with inconsistent control evidence and surprise bills. Which approach should the IS auditor BEST recommend?

options.A: Migrating every workload to the primary provider regardless of fit
options.B: Managing each cloud separately through its own native tools
options.C: Common identity, tagging and policy-as-code across every cloud
options.D: A managed service provider made accountable for the three clouds

questions.key_concept: Multi-cloud governance needs one consistent control layer across providers, with accountability kept inside the enterprise.
questions.pre_read: The problems are inconsistency and cost. Ask which option fixes those while the enterprise stays accountable.
questions.correct_explanation: The problems come from each cloud being governed differently. A common layer of federated identity, consistent tagging for cost management and policy-as-code applies the same controls everywhere and produces comparable evidence. Outsourcing to a managed service provider can bring skills and consistency, but accountability for control and compliance cannot be transferred, so the company still needs its own consistent governance.

wrong_explanations.A: Forced consolidation ignores workload fit and creates lock-in, solving inconsistency by removing choice rather than governing it.
wrong_explanations.B: Separate native tooling is exactly what causes inconsistent evidence, missing cross-cloud context and unexpected costs.
wrong_explanations.D: An MSP can operate the clouds, but accountability cannot be contracted away; the company still needs consistent controls and evidence of its own.

tips: Eliminate: A forces consolidation regardless of fit and B keeps the fragmented approach that causes the problem.
Final two: C beats D because accountability cannot be outsourced; the company needs consistent controls it owns.
Exam cue: when an option hands a provider full responsibility, remember that accountability always stays with the enterprise.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Cloud Computing Management Audit/Assurance Program; CSA Cloud Controls Matrix; COBIT 2019 APO13 (Managed Security); COBIT 2019 APO06 (Managed Budget and Costs); FinOps Foundation Framework
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Multi-cloud governance synthesis (2.9.3 depth) - unifying layer approach, complements d2_014/d2_053/d2_057/d2_067 (other cloud angles)'. Public source: ISACA Cloud Risk Management + CSA CCM + FFIEC. All scenario specifics (media company AWS/Azure/GCP split) invented for this question. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.subtopic: IT Investment ROI under Regulatory Uncertainty
questions.question: A bank is weighing a $50M AI lending platform whose ROI depends on two pending regulations. Which evaluation approach should the IS auditor BEST recommend?

options.A: Rejecting the investment until both regulations are finalized
options.B: Scenario-based ROI for each regulatory outcome, valuing modularity
options.C: The base-case ROI tested against a higher, risk-adjusted hurdle rate
options.D: Vendor indemnities shifting future compliance costs to the vendor

questions.key_concept: When specific uncertainties drive value, model each scenario explicitly so decision makers see costs, benefits and options under every outcome.
questions.pre_read: The uncertainty is specific and known: two regulations. Ask which approach shows how each outcome changes the case.
questions.correct_explanation: The uncertainty is specific: two regulations that may or may not take effect. Scenario-based ROI models costs and benefits for each outcome and values the flexibility of a modular design, so the board can decide in line with its risk appetite. A higher hurdle rate does reflect risk, but it blends both regulations into one number and hides which outcome drives the result.

wrong_explanations.A: Rejecting outright avoids rather than manages the risk and forfeits value that may hold under several outcomes.
wrong_explanations.C: A single risk-adjusted rate blurs distinct regulatory outcomes, so decision makers cannot see what drives the risk or plan responses.
wrong_explanations.D: Indemnities may recover some costs, but the bank stays accountable for compliant credit decisions.

tips: Eliminate: A avoids the decision and D tries to transfer an obligation the bank cannot hand off.
Final two: B beats C because explicit scenarios show how each regulation changes value; one higher rate hides it.
Exam cue: when named uncertainties drive an investment, prefer scenario analysis that informs the board's risk appetite decision.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 APO05 (Managed Portfolio); ISACA Risk IT Framework
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'IT Investment ROI under regulatory uncertainty analysis - multi-scenario + optionality, distinct from d2_026 (R/G/T tier discipline) and d2_068 (mid-year rebalance)'. Public source: COBIT 2019 APO05. All scenario specifics (bank AI lending platform under proposed regulations) invented for this question. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: Budget covers treatment for 11 of 18 high-priority risks, four of which face regulatory deadlines. Which prioritization should the IS auditor BEST recommend to the CRO?

options.A: The 11 highest-impact risks, regardless of category or deadline
options.B: Deferring treatment until next year's budget is approved
options.C: Cyber insurance bought instead of the treatment program
options.D: Regulatory deadlines first, then expected loss, escalating the rest

questions.key_concept: Under budget limits, treat mandatory obligations first, rank the rest by expected loss, and escalate untreated risk for formal acceptance.
questions.pre_read: Impact is only half of risk. Also ask what is mandatory and who must accept the risks left untreated.
questions.correct_explanation: Regulatory deadlines are mandatory, so they come first. The remaining budget goes to risks with the highest expected loss, which weighs likelihood as well as impact, and cheap quick wins can stretch coverage. Untreated risks are escalated so the board formally accepts or funds them. Ranking by impact alone ignores likelihood and could leave a regulatory deadline unmet.

wrong_explanations.A: Impact alone ignores likelihood and treatment cost, and could leave a mandatory regulatory deadline unaddressed.
wrong_explanations.B: Deferral leaves all 18 risks untreated, including those with fixed regulatory deadlines.
wrong_explanations.C: Insurance can transfer some financial loss, but not regulatory obligations or most operational and reputational harm.

tips: Eliminate: B leaves every risk untreated and C cannot transfer regulatory obligations.
Final two: D beats A because expected loss weighs likelihood too, mandatory items come first, and leftover risk goes to the board.
Exam cue: when resources are short, look for the option that prioritizes by risk and escalates residual risk for acceptance.
questions.framework_ref: ISO 31000:2018 (Risk Management); ISACA Risk IT Framework; COBIT 2019 APO12 (Managed Risk)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Risk Treatment under budget constraints analysis - tiered prioritization, distinct from d2_022 (foundational treatment options) and d2_070 (multi-option treatment scenario)'. Public source: ISO 31000:2018 + ISACA Risk IT. All scenario specifics (regional health insurer 18-risk register) invented for this question. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.subtopic: Auditing IT Governance Implementation. Deep Dive
questions.question: An IS auditor finds a well-designed IT governance framework, but minutes, strategy refreshes and risk reports show most required steps were skipped for years. What should the auditor BEST report?

options.A: An overall finding that governance operates in form, not substance
options.B: Separate findings for each lapse, with no overall conclusion
options.C: A satisfactory opinion, since the governance design is sound
options.D: Informal verbal feedback to the CIO instead of a written report

questions.key_concept: When several lapses share one cause, the auditor reports the pattern, here governance that operates in form only, supported by evidence for each lapse.
questions.pre_read: Look past the separate symptoms. Ask what single conclusion the board needs about whether governance actually works.
questions.correct_explanation: Several lapses with one cause show governance operating in form only. Reporting that as the main finding, supported by evidence for each lapse, tells the board its governance is not effective and drives a root-cause response. Separate findings are accurate and each needs action, but listing them without an overall conclusion invites piecemeal fixes and hides the systemic failure.

wrong_explanations.B: Each lapse is real, but reporting them only separately hides their common cause and leads to symptom-level fixes.
wrong_explanations.C: Good design does not prove effective operation. The evidence shows the framework is not working in practice.
wrong_explanations.D: Material governance gaps must be reported in writing to those charged with governance, not handled informally.

tips: Eliminate: C ignores evidence of ineffective operation and D avoids the required written report.
Final two: A beats B because a shared root cause is a systemic finding the board must see, not a list of separate lapses.
Exam cue: when many issues share one cause, the auditor reports the pattern and its root cause, with each issue as evidence.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1401 (Reporting); ISACA IT Audit Standard 1205 (Evidence); COBIT 2019 EDM01 (Ensured Governance Framework Setting and Maintenance)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Auditing IT Governance Implementation analysis - design-implementation gap synthesis, complements d2_010 (governance design vs implementation divergence at lower complexity)'. Public source: ITAF 1202 + COBIT 2019 EDM01. All scenario specifics (manufacturing conglomerate four-finding pattern) invented for this question. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: A board asks its IS auditor what distinguishes a true IT risk management program from periodic risk exercises. Which feature BEST does so?

options.A: A yearly risk list of known threats sent to senior leadership
options.B: Quarterly compliance checklists completed for the external auditors
options.C: Continuous risk assessment and treatment within board-set appetite
options.D: Ongoing vulnerability scanning and remediation by the security team

questions.key_concept: An IT risk management program is a continuous cycle of identifying, assessing, treating and monitoring IT risk against board-approved appetite.
questions.pre_read: Two options are continuous. Ask which one covers all IT risk and ties it to what the board will accept.
questions.correct_explanation: An IT risk management program is a continuous, structured cycle: risks are identified, assessed, treated and monitored, and decisions are judged against the appetite and tolerance the board has set. That ties IT risk to business objectives. Ongoing vulnerability scanning is continuous too, but it covers only technical weaknesses, is owned by one team, and does not link to the enterprise's risk appetite.

wrong_explanations.A: A yearly list is a point-in-time exercise with no treatment, monitoring or link to risk appetite.
wrong_explanations.B: Compliance checklists show conformity to frameworks, not whether IT risk is being managed to the enterprise's appetite.
wrong_explanations.D: Scanning is one technical control activity. It does not cover strategic, operational or third-party IT risk, or link to appetite.

tips: Eliminate: A is a once-a-year snapshot and B is compliance box-ticking for auditors.
Final two: C beats D because a program covers all IT risk against board-set appetite; scanning is one technical activity.
Exam cue: a risk management program is continuous, enterprise-wide and anchored to risk appetite; one team's tool is not a program.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Risk IT Framework; COSO ERM (2017); ISO 31000:2018 (Risk Management); COBIT 2019 APO12 (Managed Risk)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Risk Management Program foundational definition - continuous + structured + lifecycle, distinct from d2_011 (program components) and d2_058 (program standup governance design)'. Public source: ISACA Risk IT + COSO ERM + ISO 31000. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.subtopic: Lawful Basis for Processing. GDPR Article 6 Categories
questions.question: A privacy officer is documenting which GDPR Article 6 grounds could justify a new processing activity. Which list BEST matches those grounds?

options.A: Lawfulness and fairness, purpose limitation, data minimization, storage limitation, accuracy
options.B: Consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, legitimate interests
options.C: Govern, identify, protect, detect, respond, and recover security functions
options.D: Confidentiality, integrity, availability, authenticity, non-repudiation, and accountability of data

questions.key_concept: GDPR Article 6 lists six lawful bases: consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task and legitimate interests.
questions.pre_read: Separate the grounds that make processing lawful from the principles that govern how processing is done.
questions.correct_explanation: Article 6 sets out six lawful bases, and every processing activity needs at least one: consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task or legitimate interests. The officer records the chosen basis for the activity. The Article 5 principles, such as purpose limitation and data minimization, are also mandatory, but they govern how processing is carried out, not whether a lawful ground exists.

wrong_explanations.A: These are Article 5 processing principles. They apply to all processing but are not the Article 6 lawful grounds.
wrong_explanations.C: These are the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 functions, a security model unrelated to GDPR lawful bases.
wrong_explanations.D: These are information security properties. They describe protection goals, not legal grounds for processing.

tips: Eliminate: C is the NIST Cybersecurity Framework and D lists security properties; neither is a GDPR legal ground.
Final two: B beats A because Article 6 lists grounds that make processing lawful, while Article 5 sets principles for how it is done.
Exam cue: lawful basis answers 'may we process at all?'; principles answer 'how must we process?'.
questions.framework_ref: GDPR Article 6 (Lawfulness of Processing)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'GDPR Article 6 lawful-basis enumeration foundational - six categories recall, complements d2_040 (application - matching basis to use case)'. Public source: GDPR Article 6. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: An IS auditor must confirm that a payroll provider met its SLA targets last quarter. Which evidence is MOST reliable?

options.A: Provider's monthly SLA report, attested by its service owner
options.B: A satisfaction survey of payroll users across departments
options.C: The signed SLA document showing the agreed targets
options.D: Customer-side measurements reconciled to the defined SLA metrics

questions.key_concept: SLA compliance is best shown by customer-side measurements against defined metrics; provider reports need independent verification.
questions.pre_read: Ask who produced each piece of evidence and whether it measures actual delivery.
questions.correct_explanation: Evidence the customer generates independently, such as its own timing records reconciled to the SLA's defined metrics, shows whether targets were actually met. The provider's report is the tempting runner-up because it addresses the right targets, but it is self-reported by the party being measured; the customer should verify it rather than rely on it alone.

wrong_explanations.A: Provider reports, even attested by its own service owner, come from the party being measured. Without independent verification they cannot confirm the targets were met.
wrong_explanations.B: Satisfaction reflects perception, not measured performance against agreed targets. Users can be content while targets are missed.
wrong_explanations.C: The signed SLA shows what was promised, not what was delivered. It is the baseline for testing, not evidence of performance.

tips: Eliminate: B measures perception rather than performance, and C shows the commitment, not whether it was met.
Final two: D beats A because independent customer-side data is more reliable than a report from the party being measured.
Exam cue: for SLA compliance, prefer evidence the customer generates or verifies over provider self-reporting.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 APO09 (Managed Service Agreements); ITIL 4 Service Level Management practice
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'SLA foundational definition - documented commitment + measurable + remediable, complements d2_079 (vendor SLA design) and d2_083 (APO09 service agreements multi-element)'. Public source: COBIT 2019 APO09 + ITIL 4. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem. v2: retargeted to SLA evidence reliability to avoid duplicating d2_079.

questions.subtopic: Risk Management Program. Component Maturity Assessment
questions.question: An IS auditor assesses whether a credit union's IT risk management program is operating at a mature level. Which evidence is MOST convincing?

options.A: Assessment results visibly shaping investment and project decisions
options.B: A complete risk register with a named owner for each risk
options.C: A newly hired risk officer with strong industry credentials
options.D: A leading vendor's risk platform configured for the workflow

questions.key_concept: A mature risk program shows in behaviour: risk information actively changes business decisions, beyond having registers, staff or tools.
questions.pre_read: Note the word operating. Separate evidence that the program exists from evidence that it changes decisions.
questions.correct_explanation: Maturity in operation shows when risk information actually changes decisions: investments, projects and operational choices are visibly shaped by risk assessments. That proves the program works, not just that it exists. A complete register with named owners is an important artifact and shows sound design, but a register can be filled in once and then ignored when decisions are made.

wrong_explanations.B: A register with owners shows the program is designed, but it can exist without risk information ever influencing decisions.
wrong_explanations.C: A qualified risk officer is an input. Credentials do not show the program is working across the enterprise.
wrong_explanations.D: A configured platform is a tool. Having it says nothing about whether risk drives decisions.

tips: Eliminate: C is a staffing input and D is a tool purchase; neither shows the program working.
Final two: A beats B because operating maturity shows in decisions changed by risk, while a register proves only design.
Exam cue: for maturity or effectiveness questions, prefer evidence of behaviour and outcomes over artifacts, people or tools.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Risk IT Framework; COSO ERM (2017); COBIT 2019 APO12 (Managed Risk)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Risk Management Program maturity assessment - operational behavior over artifact/staffing/tool, complements d2_011 (program structure) and d2_058 (standup design)'. Public source: ISACA Risk IT. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: An IS auditor reviews a manufacturer's ERP rollout across 12 plants. Which stakeholder practice MOST strongly supports user adoption?

options.A: A single company-wide email at launch, cascaded by plant managers
options.B: A fast rollout with minimal notice, handling concerns after go-live
options.C: Engagement planned for each stakeholder group, with two-way feedback
options.D: Thorough end-user training delivered at each of the plants before go-live

questions.key_concept: Organizational change succeeds when stakeholders are analysed, engaged in ways that fit each group, and heard through ongoing two-way feedback.
questions.pre_read: Adoption depends on people accepting the change, not just knowing how to use it. Look for engagement that listens.
questions.correct_explanation: COBIT 2019 BAI05 treats adoption as a people problem. Analysing stakeholder groups, planning engagement around each group's concerns and keeping two-way feedback open throughout builds commitment and surfaces resistance early. End-user training is essential, but it builds skills in a one-way flow and does not address why different plants or roles might resist the change.

wrong_explanations.A: One broadcast email is one-way and untailored, and relies on managers cascading the message at their discretion.
wrong_explanations.B: Rushing with little notice increases resistance and leaves concerns to fester until after go-live.
wrong_explanations.D: Training builds skills but is one-way. It does not uncover or address each group's concerns or resistance.

tips: Eliminate: A is a single untailored broadcast and B deliberately limits communication.
Final two: C beats D because adoption needs commitment as well as skill; training alone does not engage concerns.
Exam cue: for change adoption, pick the option that analyses and engages stakeholders two ways, not just informs or trains them.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 BAI05 (Managed Organizational Change)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Enterprise Change Management stakeholder discipline - structured/tailored/two-way, distinct from d2_019 (failed M&A integration analysis)'. Public source: COBIT 2019 BAI05. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.subtopic: Data Inventory. Refresh and Drift Detection
questions.question: An IS auditor reviews how a healthcare technology firm keeps its data inventory accurate over time. Which mechanism MOST effectively detects inventory drift?

options.A: An annual survey asking units to report new or retired data
options.B: Recurring discovery scans reconciled to the inventory by data stewards
options.C: Business units notifying data governance whenever data flows change
options.D: Inferring data locations from the IT asset management database

questions.key_concept: Inventory drift is caught by independent, recurring reconciliation between what discovery finds and what the inventory records, followed up by stewards.
questions.pre_read: Note the word detects. Ask which mechanism would find data nobody remembered to report.
questions.correct_explanation: Drift is data that exists but is not recorded, or records for data that no longer exists. Recurring discovery scans reconciled to the inventory find both, independent of anyone remembering to report, and data stewards resolve the differences. Business unit notification is a sound preventive habit, but it relies on people reporting every change and cannot detect shadow data they miss.

wrong_explanations.A: An annual survey depends on memory and leaves up to a year of undetected drift.
wrong_explanations.C: Notification is useful but depends on people reporting every change, so it cannot detect the flows they forget or do not know about.
wrong_explanations.D: An asset database records systems, not the data held inside them, so it cannot reveal data drift.

tips: Eliminate: A relies on yearly recall and D tracks systems rather than data.
Final two: B beats C because independent reconciliation finds unreported data, while notification depends on people remembering.
Exam cue: when the stem asks what detects a gap, prefer an independent check over reliance on self-reporting.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 APO14 (Managed Data); DAMA-DMBOK 2nd Edition
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Data Inventory refresh and drift detection - continuous mechanisms, complements d2_016 (classification approach) and d2_076 (initial inventory build methodology)'. Public source: ISACA Data Governance + DAMA-DMBOK. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: A SaaS firm's management is embedding privacy by design into its SDLC to meet GDPR Article 25. Which practice is MOST effective?

options.A: A privacy governance review of each feature shortly before launch
options.B: Privacy controls applied to features handling sensitive data
options.C: Privacy defects found after launch fixed through bug tracking
options.D: Privacy requirements and gating criteria at every SDLC stage

questions.key_concept: Data protection by design means privacy is built in from requirements onward, with checks at each stage, not inspected in at the end.
questions.pre_read: Notice the words by design. Ask which option acts at the start of development rather than at or after launch.
questions.correct_explanation: Article 25 expects data protection to be considered when the means of processing are determined, then carried through the build. Privacy requirements and stage gates across the SDLC do exactly that. A pre-launch review is a single late checkpoint: design choices are already fixed, so problems are costly to correct and often get accepted rather than designed out.

wrong_explanations.A: A late governance review inspects privacy rather than designing it in. Architecture decisions are already made, so fixes become expensive trade-offs.
wrong_explanations.B: Article 25 covers all personal data processing, not just special categories. Ordinary personal data still needs protection by design.
wrong_explanations.C: Fixing defects after release is reactive. Personal data may already be exposed before the bug is triaged.

tips: Eliminate: B ignores ordinary personal data, and C treats privacy as a post-release defect.
Final two: D beats A because by design means building privacy in from requirements, while a launch review only inspects a finished design.
Exam cue: for anything by design, prefer the option that starts earliest and repeats through the lifecycle.
questions.framework_ref: GDPR Article 25 (Data Protection by Design and by Default); EDPB Guidelines 4/2019 (Art. 25)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'Privacy by Design SDLC integration - multi-stage embed with gating, complements d2_086 (Privacy by Design vs Default decision) and d2_084 (DPIA for high-risk processing)'. Public source: GDPR Article 25 + EDPB Guidelines 4/2019. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: A holding company subject to HIPAA, SOX and GDPR is designing a data retention policy. Which retention approach is BEST for management to adopt?

options.A: Retention periods per data category, each with a documented basis
options.B: One period for every data type, set by the longest legal requirement
options.C: One period for every data type, set by the shortest legal requirement
options.D: Retention settings left at the storage vendor's general-business defaults

questions.key_concept: Retention should be set per data category with a documented basis, meeting each law's minimum without over-retaining personal data.
questions.pre_read: Notice the three regimes pull in different directions. Ask which approach satisfies both minimum retention and storage limitation.
questions.correct_explanation: Each regime sets different obligations: HIPAA and SOX impose minimum retention, while GDPR forbids keeping personal data longer than necessary. Category-based periods with a documented basis satisfy every rule at once. A blanket longest period looks safe for compliance, but it over-retains personal data, breaching GDPR storage limitation and enlarging breach exposure.

wrong_explanations.B: Keeping everything for the longest period breaches GDPR storage limitation and increases the volume of data at risk in a breach.
wrong_explanations.C: The shortest period destroys records that HIPAA and SOX require to be kept, creating direct legal violations.
wrong_explanations.D: Vendor defaults reflect no legal analysis. Retention is a business and legal decision, not an infrastructure setting.

tips: Eliminate: C breaks minimum retention laws, and D hands a legal decision to vendor defaults.
Final two: A beats B because category periods meet every law, while a blanket maximum breaches GDPR storage limitation.
Exam cue: when regulations conflict, look for the option that classifies first and applies the right rule per category.

questions.question: An IS auditor at a community bank reviews due diligence for a new cloud-hosted core banking provider. Which approach is MOST appropriate?

options.A: A short questionnaire completed by the provider's sales team
options.B: The provider's SOC 2 Type 2 report as the main assurance source
options.C: Criticality-scaled review of finances, resilience and compliance
options.D: Assessment of the provider's risk posture after go-live

questions.key_concept: Due diligence depth should match vendor criticality. A core banking provider needs financial, resilience, compliance and contractual review, not one artifact.
questions.pre_read: Notice the vendor runs core banking. Ask whether one report can answer every risk a critical provider brings.
questions.correct_explanation: A core banking provider is a critical third party, so due diligence must be proportionate: financial viability, security, business continuity, regulatory compliance and audit rights. A SOC 2 Type 2 report is valuable evidence on controls, but it says nothing about financial health or exit, and its scope is set by the vendor. Relying on it alone under-examines a critical dependency.

wrong_explanations.A: A sales-completed questionnaire is unverified self-assertion. It gives almost no assurance for a critical provider.
wrong_explanations.B: A SOC 2 report covers selected controls in a vendor-defined scope. It does not address financial viability, continuity or contract terms.
wrong_explanations.D: Assessing after go-live removes the chance to decline or negotiate. Due diligence must come before commitment.

tips: Eliminate: A relies on unverified sales answers, and D assesses only after the bank is committed.
Final two: C beats B because a critical vendor needs risk-proportionate review across several areas; one SOC 2 report covers only part of the risk.
Exam cue: vendor oversight scales with criticality; the most critical vendors get the broadest due diligence before signing.

questions.question: After a 40% rise in cloud spend, an IS auditor reviews cost governance at a media company. Which practice MOST supports lasting cost discipline?

options.A: A hard spend cap at last year's average, regardless of demand
options.B: Tagged cost visibility, with each team answerable for its spend
options.C: An annual volume discount negotiated with the cloud provider
options.D: Cloud provisioning centralized in the CIO's office to curb spending

questions.key_concept: FinOps builds cost discipline through visibility and accountability: tag spend, allocate it, and make consuming teams own it.
questions.pre_read: Notice the word lasting. Ask which option changes behavior over time rather than applying a one-off brake.
questions.correct_explanation: Lasting discipline needs teams to see what they spend and be accountable for it. Tagging gives allocation and visibility; making each team answerable turns that into decisions such as rightsizing. Centralizing provisioning in the CIO's office can slow spend, but it moves accountability away from the consumers, creates a bottleneck for the business, and still lacks the cost visibility needed to optimize.

wrong_explanations.A: A fixed cap ignores business demand and may block legitimate growth. It limits spend without explaining or reducing waste.
wrong_explanations.C: A discount lowers the unit rate but leaves wasteful consumption untouched. Spend keeps rising with usage.
wrong_explanations.D: Central provisioning creates a bottleneck and removes accountability from the teams that consume resources, without improving cost visibility.

tips: Eliminate: A caps spend blindly against demand, and C cuts rates but not wasteful use.
Final two: B beats D because accountability belongs with the teams that consume; centralizing control slows delivery without creating cost ownership.
Exam cue: for sustained cost control, pick visibility plus team accountability over caps, discounts or central gatekeeping.

questions.question: After a phishing-led ransomware incident, an IS auditor reviews a law firm's security awareness program. Which design MOST improves staff resilience?

options.A: Annual online training for every employee, tracked by completion rate
options.B: Awareness training limited to IT staff and senior partners
options.C: Stronger email filtering in place of user awareness training
options.D: Role-based training with phishing simulations and behavior metrics

questions.key_concept: Awareness programs succeed when they change behavior, measured through simulations and metrics, not when they only record course completion.
questions.pre_read: Notice the word resilience. Ask which option measures whether staff actually resist phishing.
questions.correct_explanation: Resilience is a behavior, so the program must practice and measure it. Role-based content, simulated phishing with feedback and behavior metrics show whether staff now spot and report attacks, and guide improvement. Annual training with completion tracking is common and covers everyone, but completion proves attendance, not changed behavior, and once a year is too infrequent to sustain vigilance.

wrong_explanations.A: Completion rates show attendance, not resistance to phishing. A single yearly session fades quickly and gives no behavior evidence.
wrong_explanations.B: Phishing targets every employee. Leaving most staff untrained leaves the most common entry point open.
wrong_explanations.C: Filters reduce volume but some phishing always gets through. Technical controls complement, not replace, user awareness.

tips: Eliminate: B leaves most staff untrained, and C drops awareness in favor of filters that phishing still bypasses.
Final two: D beats A because simulations and behavior metrics prove resilience, while completion rates only prove attendance.
Exam cue: when asked about effectiveness, choose the option that measures outcomes over the one that counts activity.

questions.subtopic: Business Continuity vs Disaster Recovery. Governance Distinction
questions.question: An IS auditor finds that a bank's continuity program consists solely of IT disaster recovery plans. Which gap is the GREATEST concern?

options.A: Business process recovery priorities and workarounds are not defined
options.B: Server recovery time objectives were not tested last year
options.C: The recovery plans use a different template from other policies
options.D: The recovery team meets quarterly rather than every month

questions.key_concept: Business continuity is the broader business discipline; disaster recovery is its IT subset. DR plans alone cannot keep business processes running.
questions.pre_read: Notice the program contains only IT recovery plans. Ask what a business needs that restoring systems does not provide.
questions.correct_explanation: Disaster recovery restores technology; business continuity keeps critical business functions operating, with priorities, manual workarounds, people and communications. A program built only on DR plans has no basis for deciding what to recover first or how to operate meanwhile. Untested recovery objectives are a real DR weakness, but they are a gap within the IT subset, not a missing discipline.

wrong_explanations.B: Untested recovery objectives weaken DR assurance, but this is a quality gap inside the IT plans rather than a missing business continuity layer.
wrong_explanations.C: A template difference is a documentation style issue. It does not affect the ability to recover.
wrong_explanations.D: Meeting frequency is a minor operating choice. Quarterly meetings can be adequate if plans are maintained.

tips: Eliminate: C is a formatting point, and D is a minor meeting-cadence choice.
Final two: A beats B because missing business continuity leaves no recovery priorities at all, while untested objectives weaken only the IT subset.
Exam cue: business continuity is the parent and disaster recovery the IT child; a missing parent outranks a flaw in the child.
questions.framework_ref: ISO 22301:2019 Security and resilience — Business continuity management systems; NIST SP 800-34 Rev 1 Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems; COBIT 2019 DSS04 (Managed Continuity)

questions.question: An IS auditor reviews the audit committee charter of an NYSE-listed company. Which composition provision BEST meets the regulatory minimum?

options.A: Members drawn from senior executives with deep system knowledge
options.B: At least three members, with a majority being independent directors
options.C: Three or more independent members, one with financial expertise
options.D: A chair who appoints the other members at their own discretion

questions.key_concept: Listed-company audit committees need at least three independent directors, with financial-expert status disclosed, so oversight stays independent of management.
questions.pre_read: Notice the committee oversees management's reporting. Ask which composition keeps every member independent of the people being overseen.
questions.correct_explanation: NYSE rules require at least three members, all independent, with at least one having accounting or financial management expertise; SOX Section 407 requires disclosure of whether a financial expert serves. A mostly independent committee looks close, but any non-independent member can influence oversight of management's own reporting, which defeats the purpose of the committee.

wrong_explanations.A: Executives would oversee their own reporting. Audit committee members must be independent of management.
wrong_explanations.B: A majority is not enough. Every member must be independent, because one conflicted member can weaken oversight of management.
wrong_explanations.D: Discretionary appointment ignores independence and expertise requirements. Membership is set by the board under listing rules, not the chair alone.

tips: Eliminate: A puts management on its own oversight body, and D lets the chair bypass independence rules.
Final two: C beats B because every member must be independent of management, with financial expertise on the committee; a mostly independent committee still carries conflicted members.
Exam cue: for oversight bodies, independence from those being overseen outranks operational knowledge or convenience.

questions.subtopic: Enterprise Change Management. Failed M&A IT Integration Synthesis
questions.question: After a fast, IT-led acquisition integration lost revenue and key staff, the CFO asks an IS auditor for advice. Which recommendation is BEST for future integrations?

options.A: Keep the IT-led approach, since the systems cut over on schedule
options.B: Business-led change governance with phased cutover and go/no-go gates
options.C: An external advisory firm engaged to run future integrations end to end
options.D: A pause on acquisitions until integration capability is built

questions.key_concept: M&A integration is enterprise change: business leadership, phased cutover and go/no-go gates judged on business outcomes, not IT deadlines.
questions.pre_read: Notice the failure showed up as lost revenue and staff, not broken systems. Ask who should lead and how progress is judged.
questions.correct_explanation: The integration succeeded technically but failed the business, because IT alone drove it against a deadline. Cross-functional, business-led change governance with phased cutover and go/no-go gates judged on business outcomes addresses that cause. Hiring an advisory firm adds capacity, but accountability for integration outcomes cannot be outsourced, and the methodology gap would remain.

wrong_explanations.A: On-time cutover is not success when revenue and talent were lost. Repeating the approach repeats the failure.
wrong_explanations.C: Advisers can support, but management remains accountable. Outsourcing execution does not fix missing business ownership or gates.
wrong_explanations.D: Stopping acquisitions overreacts to a fixable method problem and may abandon the business strategy.

tips: Eliminate: A repeats the failed approach, and D abandons strategy over a fixable method gap.
Final two: B beats C because accountability for integration outcomes stays with the business; an adviser cannot own them.
Exam cue: when a change fails the business but not the technology, look for business ownership and outcome-based gates.

questions.subtopic: InfoSec Incident Response Governance. Escalation Decision
questions.question: Two hours into a ransomware attack on a payment system, it is unclear whether card data was exfiltrated. What should the information security officer do FIRST?

options.A: Brief the CEO and audit chair on facts and deadlines
options.B: Hold any escalation until the exfiltration question has been resolved
options.C: Notify every applicable regulator before the facts are established
options.D: Defer board reporting to the post-incident review meeting

questions.key_concept: Escalation is triggered by potential impact, not confirmed impact. Leadership needs early, structured facts to run legal and notification decisions in parallel.
questions.pre_read: Notice what is still unknown. Ask whether senior decisions can wait for that answer or must start alongside it.
questions.correct_explanation: A possible card-data breach starts notification clocks and legal decisions only leadership can make. A structured briefing on scope, containment, open questions and regulatory deadlines lets them act in parallel with the investigation. Waiting for certainty sounds prudent and avoids alarm, but it consumes time that notification windows do not give back and leaves accountable executives uninformed.

wrong_explanations.B: Waiting for certainty uses up notification time and keeps accountable leaders uninformed while the risk may already be material.
wrong_explanations.C: Notifying regulators before facts are known risks inaccurate statements. External notice is a leadership and counsel decision.
wrong_explanations.D: Post-incident reviews are for lessons learned. Deferring board reporting until then denies leaders decisions they must make now.

tips: Eliminate: C notifies outsiders before facts or counsel, and D defers leaders until the incident is over.
Final two: A beats B because escalation follows potential impact; leaders need facts now to run notification decisions alongside the investigation.
Exam cue: in incident questions, escalate early with structured facts; do not wait for certainty when deadlines are running.

questions.question: A bank is exiting a SaaS provider in nine months after a remediated vendor-staff access incident. Which approach should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Terminate the contract now for cause, citing the past incident
options.B: Let the contract lapse without invoking the data return clauses
options.C: Minimal vendor oversight until the contract term expires
options.D: A managed exit plan covering service, data return and deletion

questions.key_concept: Vendor offboarding is a governed process: keep the service running, enforce data return and verified deletion, and manage transition risk.
questions.pre_read: Notice the bank still needs the service for nine months. Ask which option protects both continuity and the bank's data.
questions.correct_explanation: The bank depends on the service until migration and holds contractual rights over its data. A managed exit plan keeps service levels enforced, secures data return and verified deletion, and pursues any remedies from the incident. Immediate termination feels decisive, but the incident is remediated and the new provider is not ready, so it trades a contained risk for service disruption.

wrong_explanations.A: Terminating early disrupts a service the bank still needs, for an incident already remediated. It creates a larger continuity risk.
wrong_explanations.B: Skipping data return and deletion leaves bank data with a vendor that has already shown access weaknesses.
wrong_explanations.C: Minimal oversight lets service levels slip and leaves exit obligations unmanaged during the riskiest period.

tips: Eliminate: B abandons the bank's data, and C lets the vendor drift during the exit.
Final two: D beats A because a managed exit protects continuity and data rights, while early termination trades a remediated risk for disruption.
Exam cue: at the end of a vendor relationship, choose the structured exit that keeps service and enforces data obligations.

questions.subtopic: Data Retention Conflict. GDPR vs SOX
questions.question: An EU customer requests erasure, but some of their records must be kept under SOX and national accounting-retention law. What is the BEST response for management?

options.A: Delete the customer's full record set to meet the GDPR deadline
options.B: Keep legally required records with restricted access; erase the rest
options.C: Refuse the request, since SOX retention overrides erasure
options.D: Refer the conflict to the data protection authority to decide

questions.key_concept: GDPR erasure has exemptions where a legal obligation requires retention. Keep only what the law requires, restrict it, and erase the rest.
questions.pre_read: Notice only some records carry a retention duty. Ask whether the request must be fully granted, fully refused, or split.
questions.correct_explanation: GDPR Article 17(3)(b) exempts data a controller must keep to meet an EU or member-state legal obligation, such as national accounting retention; a US law like SOX alone does not qualify. So management keeps only the required records, restricts access, erases the rest and explains this to the customer. A full refusal over-applies the exemption, and SOX alone cannot ground it under GDPR, so data no legal obligation requires would be kept.

wrong_explanations.A: Deleting records that national accounting law requires breaches a legal obligation; GDPR exempts that data from erasure.
wrong_explanations.C: The exemption covers only records the law requires. Refusing everything keeps data with no legal basis.
wrong_explanations.D: The controller must decide using GDPR's own exemptions. Supervisory authorities do not pre-rule on individual requests.

tips: Eliminate: A breaches a legal retention duty, and D passes a controller decision to the regulator.
Final two: B beats C because the legal-obligation exemption covers only required records; a full refusal retains data without basis.
Exam cue: when two laws seem to conflict, look for the answer that satisfies both by scoping, not one that picks a winner.

questions.subtopic: Risk Treatment Mid-Cycle. Newly Emerged Risk
questions.question: Mid-cycle, a critical SaaS vendor announces a business-hours outage that could halt policy issuance; the risk is absent from the approved register. What should the chief risk officer do FIRST?

options.A: Log it informally until the next quarterly register update
options.B: Accept the risk, since the outage is short and one-time
options.C: Register it now with an owner and a treatment plan
options.D: Call an emergency board meeting to approve a special budget

questions.key_concept: Risk management is continuous. A high-impact emerging risk is registered and treated when it appears, with the board informed proportionately.
questions.pre_read: Notice the risk is high impact and the outage is 90 days away. Ask whether waiting for the cycle wastes treatment time.
questions.correct_explanation: Risk management is continuous, not tied to the reporting calendar. A high-impact risk with a known date needs an owner and treatment, such as vendor negotiation and manual workarounds, while there is time to act; the board can be informed at its next meeting. An informal log preserves the cycle but leaves the risk unowned and untreated for weeks.

wrong_explanations.A: An informal log has no owner or treatment. Weeks of lead time for workarounds are lost waiting for the calendar.
wrong_explanations.B: Halting policy issuance during business hours is high impact. Accepting it without analysis or approval is unjustified.
wrong_explanations.D: An emergency board meeting is disproportionate; management can register and treat the risk and inform the board at its next meeting.

tips: Eliminate: B accepts a high-impact risk without analysis, and D escalates disproportionately.
Final two: C beats A because risk management is continuous; a known high-impact risk needs an owner and treatment now, not at the next cycle.
Exam cue: emerging risks are handled when they emerge; reporting cycles schedule updates, they do not delay treatment.

questions.subtopic: Cloud Cost Overrun. Root Cause Analysis
questions.question: An IS auditor finds cloud spend rose 60% against 25% revenue growth, with poor tagging, idle resources and unused reservations. Which recommendation is BEST?

options.A: Migrate the workloads to a cheaper cloud provider
options.B: Cap each team's cloud spend at last year's level, with CIO exceptions
options.C: Restore tagging, then remove waste with named leads in each unit
options.D: Negotiate a deeper enterprise discount with the current provider

questions.key_concept: Fix cloud overruns at the root cause: visibility first, then rightsizing and reservation use, with a named lead answerable in each unit.
questions.pre_read: Notice the evidence points to waste, not price. Ask which option addresses why spend outgrew revenue.
questions.correct_explanation: The findings show waste: untagged spend, idle resources and unused reservations. Restoring tagging separates growth from waste, and named leads in each unit then rightsize and reclaim it. A spend cap with CIO exceptions controls the total quickly, but it treats the symptom, cannot tell growth from waste, and risks starving legitimate demand while the waste stays in place.

wrong_explanations.A: Migration is costly and disruptive, and the same waste would move with the workloads to the new provider.
wrong_explanations.B: A cap limits the total without finding waste. It may block legitimate growth while idle resources keep running.
wrong_explanations.D: A discount cuts the price of waste but not the waste. Idle and oversized resources still consume budget.

tips: Eliminate: A and D act on price, while the findings show waste in consumption.
Final two: C beats B because fixing visibility and ownership removes the causes, while a cap only limits the symptom.
Exam cue: when evidence lists specific causes, choose the recommendation that addresses those causes over a blanket limit.

questions.subtopic: Crisis Communication during Major IT Incident
questions.question: Six hours into a ransomware outage of a hospital's EHR system, the CIO asks an IS auditor how to handle communication. Which approach is BEST?

options.A: Fact-based messages per audience, coordinated by the crisis team
options.B: One identical message issued to every audience through a single channel
options.C: No statements to any audience until systems are fully restored
options.D: External messages held by counsel until the investigation ends

questions.key_concept: Crisis communication is coordinated and audience-specific: each group gets the facts it needs, and statutory notices meet their deadlines.
questions.pre_read: Notice how different the audiences are: patients, clinicians, a regulator with a deadline, and the media. Ask what each needs.
questions.correct_explanation: Clinicians need workarounds, staff need scripts, the regulator needs statutory content within its window, and media need a vetted statement. Fact-based messages for each audience, coordinated by the crisis team, meet each need and stay consistent. One identical message looks consistent and simple, but it cannot carry clinical guidance or required regulatory content, so obligations and safety needs are missed.

wrong_explanations.B: One generic message cannot carry clinical workarounds or statutory regulator content. Consistency comes from coordination, not identical text.
wrong_explanations.C: Silence leaves clinicians and patients without guidance and misses the regulator's notification window.
wrong_explanations.D: Holding external messages misses the regulator deadline and leaves patients uninformed. Counsel advises; it should not block required notices.

tips: Eliminate: C stays silent past deadlines, and D lets legal review block required notifications.
Final two: A beats B because each audience needs different facts; coordination keeps audience-specific messages consistent without missing obligations.
Exam cue: in crisis communication, pick coordinated, audience-specific messaging over silence or one-size-fits-all statements.

questions.question: An IS auditor reviews the business case for a $20M data modernization program. Which element MOST supports a well-founded investment decision?

options.A: A vendor-prepared cost model showing a three-year payback period
options.B: A successful small-scale demonstration by the engineering team
options.C: Written support from every business-unit vice president before funding
options.D: Outcome-based benefits with measurable success criteria

questions.key_concept: A sound business case links quantified benefits to business outcomes and defines success measures, so value can be judged and later tracked.
questions.pre_read: Notice the phrase well-founded. Ask which element lets the board judge and later verify business value.
questions.correct_explanation: Investment decisions should rest on expected business value. Benefits tied to specific outcomes, with measurable success criteria, let decision-makers compare options and later confirm the value was delivered. A vendor cost model gives financial figures that look rigorous, but it was prepared by an interested party, is unvalidated, and speaks to cost recovery rather than business outcomes.

wrong_explanations.A: The model comes from a party that benefits from the sale and has not been independently validated. Payback alone ignores business outcomes.
wrong_explanations.B: A small demonstration shows technical feasibility, not business value or scalability.
wrong_explanations.C: Sponsorship signatures show support, not evidence. Approval without analysis is not an evidence-based decision.

tips: Eliminate: B shows only technical feasibility, and C shows support rather than evidence.
Final two: D beats A because value must be tied to business outcomes and measurable; an unvalidated vendor model is neither independent nor outcome-based.
Exam cue: for investment decisions, prefer measurable business outcomes over vendor figures, demos or signatures.

questions.subtopic: Risk Register Tooling and Workflow Design
questions.question: An IS auditor reviews the design of a new risk register tool at a bank. Which feature MOST supports the register's effectiveness over time?

options.A: Automated population of risks from incident and threat feeds
options.B: Lifecycle workflow with named owners and an audit trail
options.C: A simple shared spreadsheet maintained by the risk team
options.D: More than fifty mandatory data fields for each risk record

questions.key_concept: A register stays effective when each risk moves through a tracked lifecycle with a named owner and an audit trail of decisions.
questions.pre_read: Notice the phrase over time. Ask which feature keeps risks owned and updated after they are first recorded.
questions.correct_explanation: A register's value lies in risks being owned, treated and monitored, not just listed. Lifecycle workflow with a named owner and an audit trail keeps each risk moving and shows who decided what. Automated feeds add coverage and look efficient, but they cannot assess business impact or assign accountability, so the register fills up without being managed.

wrong_explanations.A: Feeds can suggest risks, but identification and assessment need business judgment. Automation without owners produces an unmanaged list.
wrong_explanations.C: A manual spreadsheet lacks workflow, ownership controls and change history, so it decays as the bank changes.
wrong_explanations.D: Excessive mandatory fields discourage updates. Complexity reduces adoption without improving ownership.

tips: Eliminate: C has no workflow or history, and D buries users in data entry.
Final two: B beats A because accountability keeps a register alive; automated feeds add entries but no owner or judgment.
Exam cue: for risk registers, choose ownership and lifecycle tracking over volume of data or automation.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Risk IT Framework; COBIT 2019 APO12 (Managed Risk)

questions.question: A bank's management is building a compliance program covering FFIEC, GLBA, BSA/AML and CCPA. Which design BEST supports sustained compliance?

options.A: Separate compliance teams and controls for each regulation
options.B: One control library mapped to each regulation, with named owners
options.C: The strictest regulation applied to every process as the standard
options.D: Compliance fully outsourced to a managed service provider

questions.key_concept: Integrated compliance maps one control set to many regulations, with clear owners, so overlaps are tested once and gaps are visible.
questions.pre_read: Notice the many overlapping regulations. Ask which design avoids duplication while keeping each requirement traceable.
questions.correct_explanation: Many requirements overlap across these regulations. A single control library mapped to each one lets a control satisfy several obligations, makes gaps visible, and gives each area a named owner. Separate teams per regulation bring depth, but they duplicate controls and testing, burden the business with repeated requests, and can miss cross-regulation gaps no single team owns.

wrong_explanations.A: Siloed teams duplicate controls and testing, and gaps between regulations may fall to nobody.
wrong_explanations.C: Regulations differ in scope, not just strictness. One regulation's rules do not cover another's specific requirements.
wrong_explanations.D: Providers can support, but the bank remains accountable for compliance. Outsourcing does not transfer that accountability.

tips: Eliminate: C assumes one regulation covers the others, and D tries to outsource accountability.
Final two: B beats A because one mapped control set avoids duplication and exposes gaps, while silos repeat work and miss overlaps.
Exam cue: for multi-regulation compliance, choose a unified, mapped control framework with named owners.

questions.question: An IS auditor reviews a healthcare network's IT governance committees. Which structure MOST supports effective IT governance?

options.A: One weekly committee deciding strategy, risk, architecture and change
options.B: Several committees with shared members but no written charters
options.C: The CIO deciding every IT matter directly, without committees
options.D: Distinct chartered committees with decision rights and escalation

questions.key_concept: Effective IT governance assigns distinct decisions to distinct bodies, each with a charter, decision rights and escalation path.
questions.pre_read: Notice the words effective governance. Ask which structure makes clear who decides what, and how issues move up.
questions.correct_explanation: Strategy, risk, architecture and operational change need different members, cadences and authority. Distinct committees with chartered decision rights and escalation paths give each decision a clear owner and route issues to the right level. One combined committee seems efficient for coordination, but it mixes governance with operational decisions, overloads one agenda and blurs accountability.

wrong_explanations.A: One committee mixes strategic and operational decisions, overloads the agenda, and blurs who is accountable for what.
wrong_explanations.B: Without charters, decision rights and scope are unclear, so overlap and gaps grow.
wrong_explanations.C: Concentrating every decision in one executive removes oversight and stakeholder input that governance requires.

tips: Eliminate: B lacks charters and clear decision rights, and C removes oversight entirely.
Final two: D beats A because distinct, chartered bodies give each decision clear accountability; one committee mixes governance with management.
Exam cue: good governance structures have defined charters, decision rights and escalation paths.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 (Governance and Management Roles); COBIT 2019 EDM01 (Ensured Governance Framework Setting and Maintenance); ISO/IEC 38500:2015 Information technology - Governance of IT for the organization

Public source: COBIT 2019. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: An IS auditor at a credit union reviews new outsourcing contracts. Which exit provision MOST protects the credit union's long-term interests?

options.A: Exit terms agreed at signing for data, transition and handover
options.B: A right to terminate for convenience on 90 days' written notice
options.C: Exit planning deferred until termination becomes likely
options.D: No documented exit terms, to avoid signaling expected failure

questions.key_concept: Exit strategy is negotiated before signing, when leverage is greatest: data return, transition assistance and knowledge transfer.
questions.pre_read: Notice the contracts are new. Ask when the credit union has the most leverage to secure exit support.
questions.correct_explanation: Leverage is highest before signing. Agreeing exit terms then, covering data return formats, transition assistance and knowledge transfer, means the credit union can leave without losing data or service. A termination-for-convenience right lets it leave, but says nothing about how: without transition obligations, the vendor has little reason to help a departing customer.

wrong_explanations.B: A right to leave without transition support risks lost data and service gaps. Exit needs cooperation terms, not just termination rights.
wrong_explanations.C: Once termination is likely, leverage is gone and the vendor has little reason to cooperate.
wrong_explanations.D: Exit terms are prudent risk management, not a prediction of failure. Their absence leaves the credit union exposed.

tips: Eliminate: C waits until leverage is lost, and D leaves exit undefined.
Final two: A beats B because a right to leave is not a plan to leave; transition and data terms protect continuity.
Exam cue: plan the exit at the entrance; negotiate exit support before signing, when leverage is greatest.
questions.framework_ref: FFIEC Outsourcing Technology Services booklet; ISACA Outsourced IT Environments Audit/Assurance Program; COBIT 2019 APO10 (Managed Vendors); ISO/IEC 27036-1:2021 (Cybersecurity — Supplier Relationships — Overview and Concepts)

questions.question: An IS auditor at a defense contractor reviews a new data loss prevention program. Which design feature MOST supports its effectiveness?

options.A: Blocking enforced on every egress channel regardless of context
options.B: Vendor default policies, left unchanged to reduce effort
options.C: Policies driven by data classification and tuned per channel
options.D: Monitoring of data flows with no enforcement action taken

questions.key_concept: DLP protects what is classified. Effective programs start with classification, then tune policies per channel to balance protection and usability.
questions.pre_read: Notice the program is new. Ask what DLP needs to know before it can decide what to block.
questions.correct_explanation: DLP can only protect data it can recognize, so classification comes first; policies are then tuned for email, endpoint and cloud channels and refined from false-positive analysis. Blanket blocking feels like the strongest protection for a defense contractor, but without classification it blocks legitimate work, floods analysts with alerts and drives users to unmonitored workarounds.

wrong_explanations.A: Context-free blocking disrupts legitimate work and drives users to workarounds, weakening protection overall.
wrong_explanations.B: Defaults do not reflect the contractor's own data or classification scheme, so sensitive data may go unrecognized.
wrong_explanations.D: Detection without enforcement lets sensitive data leave. It suits a tuning phase, not a mature program.

tips: Eliminate: B ignores the contractor's own data, and D watches data leave without stopping it.
Final two: C beats A because DLP must know what to protect; blanket blocking without classification disrupts work and invites workarounds.
Exam cue: for data protection controls, classification comes first; enforcement follows what is classified.

questions.question: An insurer's management plans to use a vendor's AI fraud model in claims processing. Which governance approach BEST addresses the third-party AI risk?

options.A: Reliance on the vendor's SOC 2 Type 2 report and model documentation
options.B: Independent testing on the insurer's data, plus output monitoring
options.C: In-house AI development instead, to remove vendor risk entirely
options.D: The same oversight applied to any packaged vendor software

questions.key_concept: The insurer stays accountable for AI outcomes. Third-party models need independent testing on its own data and ongoing output monitoring.
questions.pre_read: Notice the model makes decisions on the insurer's claims. Ask who is accountable if it is biased or inaccurate.
questions.correct_explanation: The insurer remains accountable for decisions the model drives, so it needs its own evidence: independent testing on its claims data for accuracy and bias, then ongoing monitoring for drift. A SOC 2 report and model documentation are useful vendor artifacts, but they cover the vendor's controls and claims, not how the model performs on this insurer's data.

wrong_explanations.A: Vendor artifacts cover the vendor's controls, not model accuracy or bias on the insurer's data. Accountability cannot be outsourced.
wrong_explanations.C: In-house models carry the same model risks. Avoiding vendors does not remove the need for testing and monitoring.
wrong_explanations.D: AI models drift and can embed bias, risks that standard software oversight does not test for.

tips: Eliminate: C assumes in-house AI carries no model risk, and D ignores drift and bias.
Final two: B beats A because the insurer is accountable for outcomes; vendor reports cover vendor controls, not performance on its data.
Exam cue: when a vendor supplies a decision model, look for independent validation and monitoring by the accountable business.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds that 60% of a holding company's IT operations spend goes to one cloud provider. Which response is BEST?

options.A: Accept the concentration as the price of negotiated discounts
options.B: Diversify across three cloud providers at once, whatever the cost
options.C: Defer analysis until a provider failure actually occurs
options.D: Weigh failure scenarios against appetite, then treat any excess

questions.key_concept: Concentration risk is managed risk-based: quantify the exposure, compare it with appetite, and mitigate only where it exceeds tolerance.
questions.pre_read: Notice the stem gives a number but no analysis. Ask what must happen before deciding whether to diversify.
questions.correct_explanation: Concentration is not automatically acceptable or unacceptable. The company should model failure, regulatory and exit scenarios, compare the exposure with risk appetite, and then mitigate where tolerance is exceeded, through exit readiness or selective diversification. Immediate multi-cloud diversification feels protective, but it commits major cost and complexity before anyone knows whether the risk warrants it.

wrong_explanations.A: Accepting without analysis is not informed risk acceptance. Discounts do not offset an unmeasured exposure.
wrong_explanations.B: Diversifying before assessment may add cost and complexity that exceed the risk itself. Treatment should follow analysis.
wrong_explanations.C: Waiting for a failure means assessing the risk only after its impact has already occurred.

tips: Eliminate: A accepts an unmeasured exposure, and C waits for the failure to happen.
Final two: D beats B because treatment should follow assessment against appetite; diversifying first may cost more than the risk.
Exam cue: assess against appetite before treating; the risk-based answer measures first, then acts proportionately.
questions.framework_ref: ISO/IEC 27036-1:2021 (Cybersecurity — Supplier Relationships — Overview and Concepts); ISACA Vendor Management Audit/Assurance Program; COBIT 2019 APO10 (Managed Vendors); COBIT 2019 APO12 (Managed Risk)
